detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in organizational decision processes through recommendations, rankings, predictions, summaries, risk assessments, and generated alternatives. Human decision-makers may nevertheless remain formally responsible for the choices that follow. Formal human involvement, however, does not reveal how the underlying judgment was formed, which influences shaped it, or whether those influences became available for examination before commitment.

This article develops a pre-decisional question: can decision-makers recognize and distinguish materially relevant influences shaping their judgment while that judgment is still being formed? It proposes Awareness of Decision Origin (ADO) as the situated recognition and differentiation of materially relevant influences shaping judgment before commitment to a consequential decision. Such influences may be internal, organizational, social, technological, or situational.

The proposed construct is positioned in relation to metacognition, source monitoring, algorithmic reliance, automation bias, human oversight, decision provenance, and emerging accounts of human agency in AI-mediated environments. Its intended distinction is not whether a person can identify the source of information, accepts or rejects AI advice, or retains formal authority. The narrower issue is whether materially relevant influences become sufficiently recognizable and differentiable to enter examination while the decision remains open.

The article establishes boundaries separating influence awareness from agency, voice, authority, decision quality, and subsequent action, and develops a staged research programe beginning with qualitative construct elicitation. Subsequent tests include discriminant and incremental validity, experimental manipulation of judgment-shaping influences, behavioral correspondence, and organizational field research.

ADO remains a conceptual proposal. Its status as a separate construct depends on future evidence that the phenomenon is coherent, empirically detectable, and sufficiently distinct from neighboring constructs. If those conditions are not supported, ADO should be narrowed, integrated with existing theory, reorganized, or abandoned.

title: Closing the Gap: Financial Supervisors’ AI Adoption
affiliations: , , Standard & Poor's and Standard & Poor's

detail.title: Closing the Gap: Financial Supervisors’ AI Adoption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Independent

detail.abstract:
Financial supervisors face a growing capability gap as financial institutions rapidly adopt artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI (GenAI), and emerging agentic AI. This paper examines the state of AI adoption among financial supervisory authorities, the structural constraints shaping adoption, and the implications for supervisory effectiveness.

The analysis draws on primary interviews with senior officials from financial supervisory authorities and financial institutions, the GovSpace State of SupTech Survey, the GovSpace corpus of live and emerging SupTech applications, and S&P Global proprietary data and research, complemented by relevant industry and policy literature. This combination of survey, interview, application-level, and financial-sector data provides both a global perspective on supervisory capabilities and a granular view of how AI is being deployed in practice.

The research finds that financial supervisors remain substantially behind the financial sector in AI adoption and maturity. While some authorities are advancing toward AI-enabled, risk-anticipatory supervision, many remain constrained by data availability and quality, legacy infrastructure, skills shortages, limited resources, data sovereignty requirements, and institutional requirements for explainability, accountability, and human oversight. The gap is particularly significant as financial institutions increasingly deploy AI in real-time and move toward more autonomous, agentic systems.

The paper proposes a maturity framework for supervisory AI adoption and examines how AI is being applied across internal operations, core supervisory functions, and the emerging supervision of AI-driven risks. It argues that closing the gap does not require supervisors to replicate the technology strategies of financial institutions. Rather, supervisors need to develop the data, infrastructure, talent, governance, and institutional capabilities required to maintain sufficient visibility into an increasingly AI-driven financial system.

title: Store-Friendly Mixed-Case Palletization: Coordinating Warehouse Packing and Store Replenishment
affiliations: , University of Science and Technology of China, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, School of Business and Management, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, NUS and NUS Business School - Department of Decision Sciences

detail.title: Store-Friendly Mixed-Case Palletization: Coordinating Warehouse Packing and Store Replenishment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Problem definition: Retail replenishment creates a supply chain coordination problem because carton packing at the distribution center (DC) affects downstream store operations. Packing cartons into fewer roll cages improves DC consolidation but can increase store replenishment effort by mixing cartons destined for distant shelf locations or splitting cartons of the same SKU across cages. We study the mixed-case palletization of store orders into roll cages, jointly determining cage assignment and physical placement to facilitate downstream store replenishment while retaining efficient DC consolidation. Methodology/results: We incorporate downstream replenishment considerations into the packing problem using pairwise walking distances between replenishment locations derived from store floor plans. These distances allow the DC to account for the spatial separation among replenishment destinations before the actual replenishment route is known. Based on this information, we introduce a co-packing distance threshold that restricts cartons destined for distant locations from sharing a cage. We show that the resulting within-cage average pairwise distance, together with cage cardinality, bounds the shortest replenishment route under packing-induced unloading precedence. We then characterize the consolidation cost of tightening the co-packing distance threshold through the resulting increase in the minimum number of cages required. To operationalize these store-side considerations within feasible three-dimensional packing, we develop a large language model-enabled extreme-point method that also promotes SKU cohesion. Managerial implications: Using real-world data from a large Singapore grocery retailer, we find that our balanced configuration uses 5.7% fewer cages than Layout Routing First Fit, a benchmark prioritizing store replenishment, while achieving nearly identical average within-cage replenishment-location distances (5.47 versus 5.48 meters). Moreover, the consolidation cost and spatial benefit of tightening the co-packing distance threshold vary across stores according to the proximity of products ordered together. Retailers can assess this proximity before packing and use it to select store-specific distance thresholds while applying the same packing method across stores.

title: Is Donation Always Beneficial? Donation and Pricing for a Socially Responsible Firm
affiliations: , University of Minnesota - Twin Cities, Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU) - International Business School Suzhou and School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University

detail.title: Is Donation Always Beneficial? Donation and Pricing for a Socially Responsible Firm

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Product donations to vulnerable populations, such as communities affected by natural disasters, pandemics, and armed conflicts, have emerged as a prominent corporate social responsibility (CSR) practice. Beyond improving the welfare of disadvantaged recipients, such donations also generate warm-glow utility for socially minded consumers, thereby raising their willingness-to-pay and reshaping market demand. This paper examines how socially responsible firms use product donations to pursue both economic and social objectives. Specifically, we examine a firm that sells its product to two segments of consumers (i.e., the primary and disadvantaged segments) and considers donation to a portion of individuals in the latter segment. Considering donation's potential warm-glow effect, the firm jointly optimizes its selling price and donation volume to maximize a weighted objective consisting of its profit and aggregate consumer surplus. By comparing the firm's optimal decisions and outcomes with a no-donation benchmark, we derive several key findings. Specifically, we show that donations achieve a "win-win" outcome for firm profitability and consumer surplus only when the firm exhibits a moderate level of social concern. When the firm's social concern becomes sufficiently high, donation may even hurt the aggregate consumer surplus. This occurs because consumers' prosocial preferences allow the firm to charge a donation-induced price premium, and the resulting loss in purchasers' surplus can more than offset the welfare gains from free access. Furthermore, a greater emphasis on consumer surplus does not necessarily raise the firm's donation volume. If the firm attaches an extremely high weight to consumer surplus, it may instead cut donation quantities and reduce its selling price to better promote consumer welfare.

title: When Critics Can Speak: Anti-SLAPP Laws and Product Quality Failures
affiliations: University of Queensland - School of Business, University of Queensland - Business School and University of Queensland

detail.title: When Critics Can Speak: Anti-SLAPP Laws and Product Quality Failures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: We examine whether legal protection for public criticism affects corporate product quality. Strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs) can deter employees, customers, journalists, and other stakeholders from communicating unfavorable information, even when the underlying claims lack merit. State anti-SLAPP laws reduce this threat by providing expedited dismissal procedures and, in many states, fee shifting. Exploiting staggered state enactments, we estimate stacked difference-indifferences models for U.S. public firms over 1996-2022. We find that anti-SLAPP enactment is associated with a 1.37-percentage-point decline in the annual probability of a product recall, equivalent to 22.1% of the sample mean. Event-study estimates show no joint evidence of differential pre-enactment trends, and the decline emerges after enactment and persists throughout the post-treatment window. The effect is stronger under more protective statutes and remains robust to alternative fixed effects, headquarters measures, event windows, reweighting, and staggered-adoption estimators. Because observed recalls reflect both the incidence and detection of defects, the negative reduced-form effect indicates that firms' preventive responses dominate any countervailing increase in defect revelation; it does not imply that stakeholder disclosure declines. Our findings identify legal protection for stakeholder criticism as an institutional determinant of product quality and demonstrate that speech protections can influence corporate operating outcomes beyond disclosure and capital markets.

title: Market Edge versus Contract Edge: Negative-expectancy Trading under an Idealized Evaluation Contract

detail.title: Market Edge versus Contract Edge: Negative-expectancy Trading under an Idealized Evaluation Contract

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, animals, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Can a trading rule lose money on average in the market yet remain valuable to a participant who buys a trading-evaluation contract? In the model developed here, the answer is yes. The trading rule does not improve; the contract changes the participant’s payoff. In the binary market benchmark, a successful market deployment earns U and an unsuccessful one loses D. These are market payoffs, not amounts paid by the provider. The baseline contract is explicitly a fictitious “50K” account with U=$3,000 and D=$2,000; the 50K label is nominal account size, not participant-deposited capital. In the idealized contract, the participant pays a fixed fee F, faces an evaluation-stage success probability p, and receives a payout W only after a second stage that succeeds with conditional probability q. Market expectancy is pU−(1− p) D, whereas participant contract expectancy is pq sW−F− p A, where s is the payout share and A is an activation fee. Under the baseline convention q= p, s=1, and A=0, the contract is positive expectancy when p>√F /W, while the market strategy is negative expectancy when p<D / (U+D). With U=$3,000, D=$2,000, F=$40, and W=$3,000, the resulting interval is approximately 11.55%< p<40%. The analysis then varies three parameters: evaluation fee F, activation fee A, and participant share s; an illustrative less-generous specification (F , A , s)=($90 ,$100 , 90%) raises the same-strategy break-even probability to 20.20% and gives expected participant cash flow of −$2 at p=q=20%. Exact finite-N enumeration gives a strict-profit probability of 87.01% for 50 baseline cycles and 40.37% for the less-generous specification. The analysis is not an arbitrage claim and does not describe any identified firm. It is the deliberately simple starting point of a wider research program on contract rules, trader heterogeneity, strategic risk, population dynamics, payout governance, and multi-account dependence.

title: LLM-derived Progress Insights from Narrative Clinical Notes for Efficient and Fair Care Allocation
affiliations: University of Waterloo, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, , ,  and

detail.title: LLM-derived Progress Insights from Narrative Clinical Notes for Efficient and Fair Care Allocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Brendan Wylie-Toal and Caterina Minaudo are employees of KidsAbility Centre for Child Development, which provided the clinical setting and data used in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study received ethics clearance through a University of Waterloo Research Ethics Board (ORE \#47450). KidsAbility Centre for Child Development authorized the use of its clinical records for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received support from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) Alliance program and Mitacs. The University of Waterloo provided facilities and institutional resources supporting the research.

detail.abstract: In longitudinal care, narrative clinical notes provide a rich record of how clients respond to treatment and change over time. While these records are central to individual care, their unstructured language and the dispersion of relevant evidence across visits make them difficult to analyze at scale. Consequently, healthcare organizations rarely use this information to support system-wide operational decisions. We develop a longitudinal progress measurement framework that combines large language model-based information extraction with clinician-grounded scoring to transform narrative clinical notes into quantitative progress trajectories. We instantiate and validate the framework in a pediatric speech-language pathology setting using real clinical documentation. We then use the resulting trajectories to demonstrate their operational value through a newsvendor-style assessment-timing model that translates heterogeneity in treatment response into differentiated assessment policies. In a retrospective counterfactual analysis, the proposed policy improves both system efficiency and the fairness of capacity allocation. More broadly, our findings demonstrate how generative AI can transform information embedded in narrative clinical notes into operational signals that support more efficient and fair allocation of healthcare capacity.

title: Time, Place, Number, Person, Environment, and Purpose: Abdur Rahman Miah's Six-Right Theory Established as an Integrated Model of Administrative Effectiveness
affiliations: Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority (BEPZA)

detail.title: Time, Place, Number, Person, Environment, and Purpose: Abdur Rahman Miah's Six-Right Theory Established as an Integrated Model of Administrative Effectiveness

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Self Financed.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A.

detail.abstract:
For decades, administrators have leaned on a simple maxim - put the right person in the right place at the right time - as though those three conditions were sufficient for an organization to run well. This study tests whether that maxim is too narrow. Drawing on Abdur Rahman Miah's Six-Right Theory, which adds three further conditions (the right number of staff, the right environment, and, above all, the right purpose) to the original three, we examined the theory as an integrated, interdependent system rather than a set of independent levers. Survey data from 428 working adults spanning thirteen countries (with Bangladesh as the largest single group) constitute the fourth and final analysis in a staged data-collection effort that began with 112 respondents and reached the study's originally planned target of 385-450.
Each of the six constructs showed good to excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha ranging from .80 to .90). Taken together as a single integrated model, the six rights accounted for 59.7% of the variance in perceived administrative effectiveness, F(6, 421) = 104.1, p < .001. This composite result remained strong and significant across all four rounds of data collection (R² from .60 to .83). Right Purpose was the only construct to predict effectiveness independently in every round (β = .25, p < .001 in the final round), consistent with its theorized role as the teleological anchor of the system. The remaining five constructs exhibited shifting individual coefficients across rounds - a pattern most plausibly explained by multicollinearity arising from their strong intercorrelations (r = .58 to .85). These intercorrelations themselves constitute empirical evidence that the six rights function as facets of an integrated whole rather than discrete, separable drivers.
The central contribution of this study is therefore the establishment of the Six-Right Theory as an integrated model of administrative effectiveness: the six conditions operate interdependently, and administrative effectiveness is the product of the system as a whole. Individual coefficients remain informative but secondary; the theory's primary claim - and the claim most robustly supported by the data - is systemic.

title: The factors behind output gap revisions
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: The factors behind output gap revisions
detail.abstract: Estimates of potential output and the output gap are widely used in monetary, fiscal and structural policy analysis, but they are unobservable and subject to substantial real-time uncertainty. This paper examines revisions to output gap and potential growth estimates produced by the European Commission, the Eurosystem, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) for the euro area and its member countries. Using annual forecast vintages covering up to 20 euro area countries from 2002 to 2025 and a balanced panel of 11 countries from 2007 to 2025, the paper compares the reliability of estimates across institutions, decomposes output gap revisions into their main sources and estimates the impact of real GDP data revisions and forecast errors on potential growth revisions. The results show sizeable differences across institutions: European Commission estimates revise least in the balanced country sample, OECD estimates revise most, and Eurosystem estimates have become markedly more stable over the past decade. Output gap revisions are driven mainly by revisions to real GDP data and potential growth, while nowcast errors play a smaller role. Panel regressions show that both real GDP data revisions and medium-term forecast errors are significantly associated with revisions to potential growth, implying that revised or unexpected GDP developments are to some extent absorbed into estimates of potential growth. The findings highlight the uncertainty surrounding real-time output gap estimates and support the use of complementary indicators of economic slack.

title: Skill or Variance? What Trading Evaluations Actually Select

detail.title: Skill or Variance? What Trading Evaluations Actually Select

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial, commercial, or personal relationships exist with any trading-evaluation provider or other organization that could reasonably be perceived as having influenced this research. The contract and population scenarios analyzed in the study are fictitious and simulated.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, personal data, or customer-level records. All trader types, population scenarios, contracts, and simulated paths are synthetic.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
Passing a trading evaluation is an outcome, not a direct measurement of trading skill. This paper makes that distinction operational with a stochastic profit-and-loss process in which trader
types differ in expected daily profit, volatility, and risk scale. Each type faces the same fictitious “50K” two-stage contract: a $3,000 target, a $2,000 drawdown, a 20-day horizon per stage, a $90 evaluation fee, a $100 activation fee, a 90% payout share, and a $3,000 gross first payout. Finite-horizon barrier probabilities are estimated using 40,000 antithetic Monte Carlo paths on a discrete intraday grid and are checked against the corresponding infinite-horizon Brownian first-passage formula. Monte Carlo uncertainty is reported from antithetic pair means. Three findings matter. First, higher variance can sharply increase the chance that a zero- or negative-drift trader completes the contract. At the baseline risk scale, the negative-drift, high-variance type passes 33.84% of evaluations, compared with 11.71% for the negative-drift, lower-variance type. The high-variance negative-drift type also has positive participant contract expectancy in the deliberately permissive model despite losing $1,500 in expected market P&L over 20 days. Second, the evaluation is an imperfect classifier. In a population containing 5% positive-drift traders and 95% zero- or negative-drift traders, 91.39% of passers and 87.30% of first-payout events come from the nonpositive group under the stated type mixture. Third, the common claim that “the losing 95% finance the winning 5%” is incomplete. With the prices and payouts used here, the provider loses an expected $137.41 per attempt in that 5/95 scenario before operating costs. The evaluation fee would need to rise from $90 to $227.41, or the gross first payout fall from $3,000 to $1,389.64, for the closed-transfer benchmark to break even. Changing the positive-drift share alone does not restore break-even under equal within-group weights: even a 1/99 population loses $121.68 per attempt. A separate population frontier shows that the variance composition of the nonpositive group is decisive. An external, vendor-reported industry funnel is used only as a calibration check: 14% reportedly obtained a funded account and 45% of that funded group received a payout, yielding roughly 6.3% before rounding. The 45% is a conditional funded-to-payout rate; the often-quoted 7% is not q. The model remains illustrative rather than an estimate of any provider’s customer base. The specific contribution is to map heterogeneous drift, volatility, and risk scale into pass composition, false selection, and provider transfer arithmetic, rather than to introduce first-passage valuation itself. Within the program, this step is necessary because the probabilities treated as inputs in the opening benchmark become outcomes of an explicit trader-type model.

title: Claude's Law Revisited: Interaction-Scale Feedback, AI-Assisted AI Research, and the Governance Time-Constant Problem
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: Claude's Law Revisited: Interaction-Scale Feedback, AI-Assisted AI Research, and the Governance Time-Constant Problem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: The central question in AI forecasting is no longer simply whether capability is improving rapidly, but whether the rate of improvement itself is beginning to accelerate. In February 2026, Claude's Law proposed that AI capability growth reflects interacting processes: human access H(t), application proliferation A(t), deployment depth D(t), productive interaction intensity I(t), and feedback-conversion efficiency F(t). This paper revisits that model against evidence accumulated during 2026 and sharpens its mathematics. The base result is exponential: if component growth rates remain constant, their product remains exponential, no matter how rapid that growth. A stronger regime requires the effective growth rate itself to rise. The paper therefore distinguishes ordinary exponential growth, an accelerating exponential regime, strict super-exponential growth, and the separate hyperbolic case produced by sufficiently strong endogenous feedback. Recent evidence remains suggestive rather than decisive. Stanford documents rapid capability, deployment, and compute growth; METR finds domain-specific acceleration in some discovery series; and Epoch AI records a capability-index slope change after reasoning models. The paper also applies its pre-specified acceleration test to METR's task-horizon series. Quadratic curvature is positive across the primary specifications and remains positive when the newest models are withheld, while a fixed September 2024 breakpoint yields substantially shorter post-break doubling intervals. However, robust residual intervals and model-set sensitivity prevent a definitive inference, and matched-model comparisons show that the change from TH1.0 to TH1.1 alters the estimated trend itself. The test therefore provides suggestive evidence of acceleration, not proof of sustained accelerating-exponential growth. AI-assisted AI research is treated as a mechanism within F(t), not as a new multiplier. The paper also identifies a control-theoretic implication: if capability cycles shorten faster than safety and governance response times, relative control lag increases even without strict super-exponential growth. A separate observability problem arises if measurement fidelity deteriorates while capability cycles shorten. Claude's Law is therefore presented as a prospective, falsifiable framework whose stronger claims remain conditional.

title: Beyond the Boardroom: Corporate Participation in Unofficial Diplomacy in Conflict Zones, Tracks Two and Three

detail.title: Beyond the Boardroom: Corporate Participation in Unofficial Diplomacy in Conflict Zones, Tracks Two and Three

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study examines how businesses engage in Track Two and Track Three unofficial diplomacy in conflict-affected environments, framing them as pragmatic peacebuilders. Moving beyond conventional depictions of firms as either purely self-interested or altruistic, the research demonstrates that business engagement is context-dependent, shaped by a combination of strategic opportunism, relational networks, technical expertise, financial capacity, and, in certain cases, value-driven considerations. Drawing on qualitative data, the study integrates insights from resource-based, stakeholder, legitimacy, institutional, and Habermasian theories to illustrate how firms leverage relational, financial, and cultural assets to influence conflict-related processes while simultaneously pursuing reputational and, occasionally, moral objectives. Engagement is often reactive and contingent, mediated by access to political networks, invitations to informal diplomatic platforms, and the firm's embeddedness in social and cultural contexts. The findings highlight that engagement outcomes are not uniform: some businesses act primarily to protect operations and enhance competitive advantage, while others are additionally motivated by cultural, ethical, or emotional proximity to the conflict. By presenting a three-layered framework combining realist and psychological-constructivist drivers, this study advances understanding of corporate diplomacy in fragile environments and offers a nuanced conception of businesses as contextually adaptive actors contributing selectively to conflict mitigation.

title: A De Facto Referendum: How Proxy Advisors Set Their Standards Through Director Election
affiliations: EDC Paris Business School, ESSEC Business School and HEC Paris

detail.title: A De Facto Referendum: How Proxy Advisors Set Their Standards Through Director Election

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding information

detail.abstract: We study the standard-setting role of proxy advisors when their preferences diverge from regulatory mandates and shareholders' choices. The say-on-pay (SOP) regulation in 2011 allowed U.S. firms to adopt non-annual voting schedules, whereas proxy advisors strongly preferred annual voting. We show that they leverage negative recommendations in compensation committee member elections (CMEs) as an alternative channel for expressing compensation-related concerns in non-SOP years. Among firms that hold triennial SOP votes, negative recommendations in CMEs are significantly more frequent during non-SOP years. Moreover, proxy advisors promote their standards even more strongly in firms where their preferences are less aligned with the voting choices of shareholders, highlighting their standard-setting role even when unpopular.

title: Opening the Black Box of Electronics Procurement: A Life-Cycle-Based Screening of Environmental and Social Supply-Chain Hotspots
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Opening the Black Box of Electronics Procurement: A Life-Cycle-Based Screening of Environmental and Social Supply-Chain Hotspots

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of competing interests The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding recieved

detail.abstract:
Electronic-product procurement is often treated as a routine administrative activity, yet laptops, smartphones, displays and desktop computers are embedded in opaque global value chains involving semiconductors, batteries, metals, hazardous chemicals, energy-intensive refining and waste treatment. This paper develops a reproducible screening approach for identifying environmental, human-health and social-risk hotspots in electronics procurement. Using Montanuniversität Leoben as an illustrative case, four openLCA/ecoinvent 3.9.1 product systems were analyzed, covering 54,983 upstream process entries across desktop computers, laptops, smartphones and displays. Process entries were classified with an expert-informed rule-based human and environmental hazard score and then overlaid with country-level Decent Living Standards and the U.S. Department of Labor list of goods associated with child and forced labor.
The results show that the full upstream model is strongly shaped by background datasets, particularly broad European regional datasets and Swiss processes, which dilute the apparent social-risk signal. While 18% of country-mapped process entries are located in countries with Decent Living Standards below 0.8, this share increases to 46.6% when the analysis is restricted to electronics-related process groups. Child- and forced-labor screening identifies 668 potentially affected process entries in 25 countries, with the strongest overlaps in India, China and Brazil. China is particularly relevant because electronics itself is flagged for child labor, forced labor and forced child labor.
The study does not claim to prove supplier-level violations. Instead, it shows how life-cycle data can turn opaque electronics procurement into a transparent set of countries, sectors and processes where due diligence must begin. Its main contribution is methodological: transforming life-cycle inventory background data from an environmental accounting tool into an early-stage sustainability and due-diligence screening layer.

title:
When Patients Become Partners: Trust, Technology, and the Future of Healthcare in Sri Lanka 
A Perspective on Artificial Intelligence, the Doctor-Patient Relationship, and Evidence-Based Integration of Traditional and Digital Health Knowledge
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title:
When Patients Become Partners: Trust, Technology, and the Future of Healthcare in Sri Lanka 
A Perspective on Artificial Intelligence, the Doctor-Patient Relationship, and Evidence-Based Integration of Traditional and Digital Health Knowledge

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Sri Lanka's healthcare system has long been recognised for achieving strong population health outcomes despite limited financial and human resources. This achievement is now being tested by two simultaneous transformations: an accelerating outmigration of experienced physicians in the wake of the country's economic crisis, and the rapid, largely unregulated adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health tools by patients themselves. This perspective article examines how these two forces are reshaping the doctor-patient relationship, moving it from a model historically grounded in professional authority towards one grounded in informed partnership. Drawing on the international literature on AI in healthcare, patient empowerment, and trust in clinical relationships, together with an integrated-flexible, case-study-informed methodology, the article develops three illustrative case studies: AI-assisted interpretation of laboratory reports, AI-supported telemedicine follow-up for chronic disease, and the evidence-based evaluation of a Sri Lankan traditional remedy (Heen Bovitiya, Osbeckia octandra) for liver disease. The discussion argues that AI is best understood not as a replacement for clinical judgement but as a decision-support and health-literacy tool that, used responsibly, can strengthen trust between doctors and patients. The article concludes with policy-relevant recommendations for healthcare professionals, hospitals, medical education, and policymakers, and situates the future of Sri Lankan healthcare as a partnership between professional expertise, informed patients, and responsibly governed technology.

title: Adaptive AI Risk Intelligence for Managing Operational Disruptions in Critical Infrastructure Systems

detail.title: Adaptive AI Risk Intelligence for Managing Operational Disruptions in Critical Infrastructure Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled analytics, predictive models, and automated decision-support systems are increasingly used to strengthen risk management and operational decision-making in critical infrastructure. However, infrastructure disruptions can arise from equipment failures, cyberattacks, environmental conditions, supply interruptions, abnormal operating states, and degraded data quality, creating conditions in which conventional AI risk systems may generate accurate predictions without adequately determining whether those predictions remain trustworthy as operational conditions change. This study addresses this gap through a systematic critical synthesis of the supplied literature on AI risk analytics, predictive intelligence, data reliability, cybersecurity, infrastructure resilience, and adaptive decision-making. The synthesized findings indicate that AI-driven analytics can improve early threat detection, predictive risk assessment, and operational response, but model performance alone does not guarantee reliable operational decisions. Effective decision confidence is influenced by data quality, cybersecurity conditions, operational context, uncertainty, and disruption severity. Based on these findings, the study proposes an Adaptive AI Risk Intelligence framework that continuously connects real-time data acquisition, reliability assessment, context and disruption assessment, predictive risk intelligence, uncertainty and confidence assessment, adaptive decision authority, and outcome monitoring and learning. The framework emphasizes that trustworthy infrastructure decisions require AI predictions to be evaluated against changing data reliability and operational context, enabling decision authority to adapt as risk and uncertainty evolve.

title: John Milton’s Areopagitica: A Scholarly Poem
affiliations: Barry University School of Law

detail.title: John Milton’s Areopagitica: A Scholarly Poem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no personal or financial relationship with any person or organization in regards to this scholarly work.
declarations.funderStatement: I received no funding with regard to this scholarly work.

detail.abstract: This scholarly poem examines John Milton’s Areopagitica (1644) and its enduring significance in the development of the freedoms of speech and press. Combining verse with historical and legal scholarship, the poem positions Areopagitica within seventeenth-century England’s system of prepublication licensing and distills Milton’s principal arguments against that system. These include the fallibility of government censors, the futility of suppressing ideas, the value of intellectual debate in the pursuit of truth, and the conception of books as living repositories of human thought. At the same time, the poem highlights important limitations often obscured in modern celebrations of Milton. First, his defense of expressive freedom was principally a rejection only of prior licensing, not an argument for immunity from punishment after publication. And second, he expressly contemplated sanctions for writings deemed libelous, seditious, or otherwise harmful. Finally, the poem traces Areopagitica’s influence beyond its unsuccessful immediate appeal to Parliament, including the transmission of Milton’s anti-licensing arguments through later writers and their contribution to the intellectual movement preceding the lapse of England’s Licensing Act in 1695. In doing so, the poem uses a hybrid form (poetry supported by scholarly annotation) to present both an accessible account of Areopagitica and a historically qualified assessment of Milton’s place in the Anglo-American free-speech tradition.

title: Achieving Hinterland Modal Shift Under Decentralized LSP Decision-Making: A Hinterland Planning Model for Port Authorities
affiliations: , Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Rotterdam School of Management (RSM) and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Rotterdam School of Management (RSM)

detail.title: Achieving Hinterland Modal Shift Under Decentralized LSP Decision-Making: A Hinterland Planning Model for Port Authorities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper
declarations.funderStatement: This project has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under Grant Agreement 101036594.

detail.abstract: Port authorities are expected to play a facilitating role for the movement of hinterland freight towards lower-emission modes, yet they do not control the shipment-level decisions of the logistics service providers (LSPs) that determine mode, route and timing. This paper develops a two-level tactical planning model that allows a port authority to evaluate policy interventions, such as environmental regulation, intermodal capacity configuration, service pricing and booking flexibility, through the decentralized operational response of multiple LSPs rather than through a centrally imposed plan. At the operational level, each LSP plans shipments over a rolling horizon, trading off transport cost, emissions and transit time under the conditions set by the tactical policies. The operational problem is formulated on a reduced network representation that substantially improves computational efficiency and makes the approach tractable for large-scale hinterland networks. The model is implemented as a decision support module within the digital twin demo developed for HAROPA Port (Le Havre-Rouen-Paris) and used for scenario-based policy evaluation. The experiments yield four managerial insights. Intermodal services can lower cost and emissions simultaneously, but time pressure shifts cargo back towards road transport. Limited intermodal capacity is the binding constraint on modal shift, but capacity expansions must be targeted rather than uniform. Pricing requires careful calibration, since both high prices and excessive subsidies distort modal choice and lead to an inefficient allocation of scarce intermodal capacity. Flexible booking improves planning efficiency, but its benefits depend strongly on coordination and diminish in fragmented markets.

title: Caring and Daring: The Window of Excellence as an Attachment-Based Map of Psychological Safety in Leadership
affiliations: De School voor Transitie (The School for Transition), De School voor Transitie (The School for Transition), De School voor Transitie (The School for Transition) and De School voor Transitie (The School for Transition)

detail.title: Caring and Daring: The Window of Excellence as an Attachment-Based Map of Psychological Safety in Leadership
detail.abstract: Psychological safety is one of the most cited and least reliably practiced ideas in management: leaders know they should create it, yet in the moments that matter it slips away. This article introduces the Window of Excellence, a practice-derived model that explains why. The window rests on the two functions of a secure base identified by attachment research, caring and daring. Where both are high, people and teams excel; where one or both fall away, three patterns emerge: To Dominate, To Avoid and To Withdraw. The model treats these quadrants as movements rather than types: under pressure, leaders leave the To Excel quadrant along paths laid down in their attachment history and can learn to notice that movement and return. We describe the model, its use with leaders, teams and coaches, and a research agenda.

title: Correcting Optimism: Informational Interventions in Affective Decision-Making
affiliations: HEC Paris, University of Valencia and Universidad de Alicante

detail.title: Correcting Optimism: Informational Interventions in Affective Decision-Making
detail.abstract: We develop a behavioral model of affective decision-making where agents hold heterogeneous baseline beliefs. By observing coverage choices in insurance markets, we reveal underlying cognitive biases: under-insurance identifies optimism, while over-insurance identifies pessimism. To correct these distortions, we introduce policy interventions designed to shift perceived probabilities toward objective truth without altering financial payoffs. Finally, we establish sufficient behavioral conditions under which these campaigns successfully increase insurance demand, demonstrating that informational nudges are highly effective for strongly risk-averse agents.

title: Analyzing Structural Adjustment Programme: Nigerian Foreign Exchange Crisis and Banking Liquidity Crisis from Mid-1980s Throughout 1990s and Beyond
affiliations: Rhema Univeristy, Nigeria.

detail.title: Analyzing Structural Adjustment Programme: Nigerian Foreign Exchange Crisis and Banking Liquidity Crisis from Mid-1980s Throughout 1990s and Beyond

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interests whatsoever as regards the authorship and publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: John Nkeobuna Nnah Ugoani is Professor of Management and Dean School of Postgraduate Studies at Rhema University, Nigeria. His research interest focuses on business, management, governance, leadership, entrepreneurship, sustainability, and emotional intelligence. John is recognized for presenting the first best PhD Thesis in Management at the Faculty of Business Administration, Imo State University, Owerri, Nigeria. He has over 200 scholarly publications with over 200,000 full paper readership downloads, and ranked among Top Ten Authors by SSRN/Elsevier. He presented the first inaugural lecture at Rhema University Nigeria. Before entering academia, he was a Senior Manager at First Bank of Nigeria Plc.

detail.abstract: Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP) conceived as a vehicle of economic reform featured economic deregulation and financial liberalization encompassing exchange rate regulation, local currency devaluation as central measures to improve national economic performance. The idea of SAP brought about increased banking competition as manifested in higher risk appetite, hence banks and consequently bank depositors were exposed to greater risks associated with banking liquidity crisis, distress and failure. Also, exchange rate crisis associated with local currency devaluation became imperative because the country had experienced chronic volatility in exchange rate which was informed by various policies of the government from the post-independence era when the country had maintained a fixed exchange rate at par with the British Pounds throughout the oil boom of the 1970s to the floating of the local currency in 1986 following the near collapse of the national economy between 1982 and 1985. Thus, the issues of devaluation, revaluation, overvaluation and undervaluation of the local currency were escalated by SAP. Any situation that exists whereby the official exchange rate is altered in a way that a unit of a country's currency can buy fewer units of foreign currency leads to a problem of devaluation. At the same time, when the official exchange rate is altered in such a way that the local currency can buy more units of foreign currency, becomes a matter of revaluation and in this circumstance, devaluation and revaluation represent the gross official responses to overvaluation and undervaluation respectively existing in a country's currency. A combination of economic deregulation and financial liberalization unleashed unique entrepreneurial banking behavior which in turn raised the levels of competition in the financial sector of the economy with implications for foreign exchange rate crisis as well as banking sector liquidity crisis. The exploratory research design was adopted for this study and the result showed significant positive relationship between SAP and foreign exchange rate crisis and banking liquidity crisis in Nigeria from the mid-1980s throughout 1990s and beyond. This work was not exhaustive due to lack of current relevant literature and research funding. Further research could examine the relationship between unemployment and the need for more government intervention in the agricultural sector in Nigeria. This study recommends that the monetary authorities should ensure transparency in fiscal policy management as an important measure of promoting national development.

detail.abstract: The article examines the role of the digital component of scientific and technological potential in ensuring the economic security of the Russian Federation. An analysis of the dynamics of spending on digital economy development in Russia for 2018-2023 is presented, showing a 44% increase despite the pandemic and sanctions pressure. The composition of technological sanctions aimed at weakening the country's technological sovereignty is also analyzed. The author concludes that under conditions of external constraints, a transition is taking place toward the use of internal reserves and systemic interaction among federal, regional, and corporate levels.

detail.title: Do German Judges Treat People With Foreign Names Differently? A Vignette Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have nothing to declare.

detail.abstract: In a realistic survey experiment with a 2x2 factorial design we submit a hypothetical but realistic assault case to 282 sitting German judges and ask whether they would open trial against the suspect (a formal procedural step in German criminal proceedings). We vary the name of the accused (Turkish vs. German) and the consistency of the evidence (consistent vs. inconsistent) independently and compare the decisions as well as some preliminary assessments of these decisions between treatments. We find neither a statistically significant effect of name on the decision to open trial nor on any of the preliminary assessments. We do find, however, a strong and significant effect of the consistency of the evidence on the decision and the assessment of the probability of the suspect's guilt. We corroborate our null result, neither finding an effect of name on the decision to open trial nor on any of the preliminary assessments despite increasing power by testing parametrically and including covariates. However, we estimate a wide null. Our data can only exclude with 95 % confidence that a Turkish name increased the probability of opening trial by more than 26 %. Also, including the interaction of name and consistency in the regression as a further robustness check, we do find a marginally significant interaction effect and a significant effect of name. Exploring the data further, we see that judges err more often to the detriment of the accused if the accused has a Turkish name. Judges with professional experience relevant to the specific case in question are less affected by the name while mere length of tenure seems not to help insulating judges from influence of the suspect's name.

detail.abstract: Clusterwise least squares partitions regression data into K groups with separate linear fits. We study a subsample ensemble: solve the problem exactly on each of B small random subsamples, extend each solution to the full sample, align the labels, and combine the replicates by a plurality vote, by averaging, or by selection. Each replicate is an empirical K-quantizer on m points, which makes an exact analysis possible. Conditionally on the data the replicates are independent and identically distributed, so the vote converges exponentially fast in B to the plurality partition of the replicate law, which coincides with the criterion minimizer outside a boundary set that does not shrink with B. For the two-group location model we show, under a partial-recovery condition, that m of order 1/π_min suffices for a replicate to be right more often than wrong. Exact minimizers for two groups and one covariate, computed in O(n^3) time, let us check each prediction. On clean data the ensemble is not a better optimizer than multistart alternation. Under gross outliers in the response, an adaptively trimmed variant needs no trimming level and had higher worst-case accuracy than trimmed alternation at any fixed level, with up to 20% contamination.

detail.abstract: Cambodia's rapid adoption of mobile banking, interoperable QR payments, and digitally mediated commerce is expanding the practical opportunities available to young people while simultaneously increasing their exposure to complex borrowing, fraud, data misuse, and behavioral risks. This paper critically synthesizes authoritative Cambodian policy documents, internationally comparable financial-inclusion evidence, peer-reviewed research on financial education, and current consumerprotection guidance. It distinguishes established evidence from unsettled questions and develops an applied research framework for Cambodian youth aged 15-30, the age range used in Cambodia's youth-development policy architecture. The evidence supports four conclusions. First, digital finance can reduce transaction costs, improve payment convenience, and support formal saving, but access alone does not guarantee financial resilience. Second, borrowing can finance education, enterprise, and emergency needs, yet weak affordability assessment, multiple borrowing, and frictionless digital credit can intensify debt stress. Third, online scams are evolving faster than consumer capability, requiring prevention, rapid response, and redress mechanisms in addition to awareness campaigns. Fourth, financial education produces positive average effects when it is timely, intensive, relevant, and linked to actual decisions, but education alone cannot substitute for fair product design, responsible lending, effective supervision, and social protection. The paper proposes a mixedmethod national study, a 2026-2028 implementation roadmap, a multi-stakeholder governance model, and a Board-level scorecard suitable for a responsible youth financial-capability initiative. Because no original participant data are analyzed, all Cambodia-specific causal claims remain research hypotheses rather than findings.

detail.abstract: We study how banking crises reshape nonbank financial institutions' (NBFIs) role in corporate debt markets using primary-market syndicated loans and corporate bonds over 1990-2025. We find that NBFI cyclicality is function-specific: NBFIs contract syndicated loans relative to banks but expand corporate bond underwriting, especially through bank-affiliated NBFIs. Firms with stronger pre-crisis NBFI underwriting relationships are more likely to switch from loans to bonds, raise more bond financing, experience smaller declines in total borrowing, and exhibit stronger crisis outcomes. This reconciles competing views of nonbank cyclicality: NBFIs may amplify stress as loan-market risk bearers while preserving market access as bond underwriters.

detail.abstract: This reflection reads the MIT Ad Hoc Committee Report on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training (August 2026) as both an important institutional intervention and an object of philosophical inquiry, and then asks what it would mean to translate that inquiry into a usable analytical framework for institutional actors who must actually produce AI policy. The reflection proceeds in three movements. The first summarizes the Report and compares its principles and recommendations with my empirical study of twelve law-school AI policies (Structure, Opacity, and Convergence), my Five Machines analysis of machine-generated policy models, My Dinner With ChatGPT's phenomenology of recursive human-machine inter-subjectivity, and my course-level AI policy. That comparison identifies convergence around contextual governance, transparency, verification, and augmentation, but also divergence over the structural axes of policy architecture, the legal character of human agency, and whether the machine can be treated only as an object of governance. The second movement, under the Nietzschean heading "Philosophising With a Hammer," develops eight analytical queries informed by phenomenological, genealogical, semiotic, and path-dependence frameworks. These queries examine the Report's foundational presuppositions, the cognitive cages within which its recommendations are generated, the gap between its transformative diagnosis and its incremental prescription, the genealogical production of its eight principles, the semiotic performance of institutional convergence, the temporal architecture of its review mechanisms, the absence of the machine as interlocutor, and the narcissistic closed loop through which the institution governs its own reflection rather than the phenomenon itself. Norbert Wiener's God & Golem, Inc.-the work of a prior generation of MIT's own intellectual tradition-serves as counterpoint: the creator-creature relation is already a significant game, and the refusal to play may be the most consequential move in a game already underway. The third movement, developed in a companion Operationalization Appendix, translates the philosophical critique into an analytical framework organized around four layers of institutional decision-making: foundational ontological commitments, second-order normative principles, structural policy architecture, and operational implementation. The appendix contends that institutions characteristically compress these layers-moving from unexamined foundational assumptions directly to operational recommendations-and that this compression is itself a mechanism of path dependence. It offers decision trees tracing the MIT Report's implicit pathway alongside alternative pathways drawn from the Five Machines study and from The Soulful Machine's ontological premises, together with a variable disentanglement chart mapping eleven critical decision points across the four layers. detail.abstract: High-dimensional fixed effects are now standard in empirical finance, but they can obscure which observations dominate identification. We show that, after accounting for saturated fixed effects, a treatment effect coefficient may be identified by a very small number of observations. We derive simple diagnostics that quantify concentration in identifying variation. In binary designs, effective sample size collapses when a small set of the data carries most residualized treatment variance. In continuous-regressor settings, identification can rely primarily on observations far in the tails of the distribution. We then propose three practical diagnostic statistics that can be easily computed and recommend reporting them for fixed effects regressions. Applying these tools to employment-protection laws, investment-q regressions, and aggregate investment concentration, we show that strong fit and statistical significance can coexist with thin and highly concentrated identification. Fixed effects are powerful empirical tools, but their identifying geometry should be reported explicitly, and care should be taken when assessing external validity in such designs.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) could become a critical tool for helping to improve access to justice for people who experience problems at work, providing better access to legal information and helping self-represented litigants draft documents and communicate to a legal audience. Drawing on a case study of AI and large language model (LLM) use in the Fair Work Commission (FWC), targeted questioning of ChatGPT, and a review of FWC cases, this article critically examines the extent to which AI is enabling access to justice, within and beyond the FWC. It offers new and innovative insights into the emerging use of AI in the FWC. The article maps the emerging problems facing the FWC associated with AI use, including rapidly growing workloads, hallucinations, verbose and incoherent submissions and documents, and growing numbers of claims with little merit. I argue that, at present, the use of AI is more likely to limit access to justice than to enable it.

detail.abstract: We examine when contracting parties produce their own measure of balance-sheet debt, deciding which obligations count as debt rather than accepting the boundary drawn by general-purpose accounting standards, and how that private recognition responds when the standard redraws it. Using generative artificial intelligence to read the debt and leverage definitions in nearly 15,000 private loan agreements from 2000 to 2025, we find that customization of lease-related debt definitions increases as borrower credit ratings deteriorate and as lenders experience adverse accounting events and defaults in their portfolios, and decreases with prior lending relationships. Customized definitions and clauses freezing GAAP are complements. Before ASC 842, 70 percent of contracts that froze GAAP customized indebtedness to capture off-balance-sheet leases, against 29 percent of those that did not. That gap narrowed substantially after ASC 842 partially aligned the public rule with the measure these contracts had privately specified, though the alignment was partial and customization did not disappear. Recognition standards appear to shape how contracting parties implement their measurement goals rather than the goals themselves.

detail.abstract: This study proposes a statistical shape model (SSM)-guided framework for reconstructing the complete external three-dimensional eyeball surface from anterior- and posterior-segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) images and measured axial length. OCT-derived ocular profiles were converted into three-dimensional point clouds, and a point-cloud-based regression network estimated the first 10 principal component coefficients of an SSM constructed from eyeball masks manually delineated on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. The predicted coefficients were decoded to generate a complete external eyeball surface. Using paired OCT–MRI data from 22 eyes of 11 participants, reconstruction accuracy was evaluated against MRI-derived reference surfaces and volumes. A test set comprising six eyes from three participants was evaluated using all five fold-specific models obtained from participant-grouped training–validation folds. After each test eye’s performance metrics were averaged across the five models, the root-mean-square distance (RMSD), absolute volume error, and signed relative volume error were 0.337 ± 0.070 mm, 629.8 ± 417.4 mm³, and -7.10 ± 4.18%, respectively (mean ± SD). Models trained with geometrically corrected posterior OCT profiles yielded a numerically higher mean test RMSD (0.354 ± 0.076 mm) than those trained with the original profiles. These results support the feasibility of reconstructing complete eyeball geometry from partial anterior- and posterior-segment OCT observations and measured axial length without requiring subject-specific MRI at inference, potentially reducing the MRI-related cost and burden of whole-eyeball shape assessment.

detail.abstract: Scheduled announcements provide clean settings for studying how public information moves Treasury yields, but much of the news flow arrives between releases. We use dictionary, topic, and large language model (LLM) methods to measure seven macroeconomic news categories from the Wall Street Journal over 1990-2022. The LLM records category presence, supporting text, and economic directions. Signed coverage raises daily yield-regression R2 by up to 1.10 percentage points beyond yield-curve controls and measured macroeconomic and monetary-policy surprises. When both the current and preceding Treasury trading sessions are free of scheduled announcements, the category block remains jointly significant from 6m through 5y. Signed inflation coverage is associated mainly with changes in the expected short-rate component, signed growth coverage with changes in both yield components, and tighter monetary-policy coverage with declines in term premia.

detail.abstract:
Since 28 May 2026, four modules of the European Database on Medical Devices (EUDAMED) have become legally mandatory for medical device manufacturers, with legacy-device registration due by 27 November 2026. For many manufacturers, the device data required for these submissions is distributed across internal systems never designed for regulatory reporting, creating a gap between internal data sources and final EUDAMED submission. While the literature addresses individual elements of this problem, the complete source-to-submission process has not been examined as a single operational pipeline.

This paper addresses that gap through a PRISMA 2020-guided systematic literature review of peer-reviewed and grey literature (Web of Science, PubMed, OpenAlex, plus structured grey-literature search of European Commission, MDCG and MedTech Europe sources), quality-appraised via CASP and AACODS. From 125 identified records, 30 met eligibility criteria (20 peer-reviewed, 10 institutional documents), analyzed through inductive thematic analysis and cross-stream triangulation.

The synthesis yields a chronological five-stage typology of data-preparation challenges: extraction, schema mapping, EMDN classification, validation, and audit-trail documentation, with governance as a cross-cutting theme. Findings suggest SMEs face a capability constraint concentrated in early pipeline stages, while large enterprises face a coordination constraint intensifying in later stages as record volume and functional complexity grow. Higher-risk devices combine greater record complexity with additional certification and clinical-documentation burden, while lower-risk devices concentrate higher registration volume. These are formulated as testable propositions rather than established findings, given the literature-based design. The paper concludes with an EUDAMED data-readiness framework, a practical self-assessment instrument, and a conceptual business model for third-party data-readiness services.

title: Do Animals Matter? The Value of Animal Welfare Information to Consumers
affiliations: Harvard Law School, University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Students, University of Cambridge and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Do people want information about animal welfare? What kinds of animal welfare information do they want, and what do they want to avoid? What motivates people to seek or avoid such information? We report the results of surveys in six countries-Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, and the United States-on people's desire to receive or not receive animal welfare information with respect to meat, milk and eggs, fur and leather products, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and pet food. We find that across all nations and products, providing such information is likely to yield substantial welfare benefits to consumers. In all contexts, substantial minorities do not want to receive such information, but significantly larger groups do. Moreover, those who want to receive the information are willing to pay significantly more for it than those who do not want to receive it would pay not to receive it. We also find significant differences across nations (but not across products). We report a wide range of correlations between social and demographic characteristics and the desire to receive or avoid animal welfare information. Investigating the motives for obtaining or avoiding animal welfare information, we find that cognitive, instrumental, and, to a lesser extent, affective motives predict whether people want to know or not to know. The affective motive, however, is the only significant predictor of how much people are willing to pay for avoidance, while both the cognitive and the affective motives predict how much people are willing to pay to receive information. People who believe that animal welfare information would induce negative affect and who do not think such information is useful or interesting do not want that information and would even be willing to pay to avoid it. These findings have evident policy implications.

detail.abstract: Before each Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, staff prepare several statements that combine current instruments, future policy, and language, while the public observes only the statement the Committee selects. These hidden menus reveal how monetary policy and its communication are designed together. I reconstruct 433 official drafts from 135 meetings and score 429 of them using a fixed large language model (LLM) procedure that generates a joint panel of 30 tenor-specific rate readings. On released statements, the dispersion of these readings ranks the magnitude of immediate repricing across futures, swaps, and Treasury markets and improves historical predictions based on earlier meetings. Applying the same procedure to the official alternatives reveals that, among drafts implementing the same current instruments, the selected statement generally supports more concentrated medium-and long-term rate readings. A second model family reproduces the direction of this ordering. The official record explains the pattern. Staff usually place the expected action and inherited language at the center of the menu, while alternatives and meeting-day revisions encode changes in the future policy path, the reaction function, and the flexibility retained by policymakers. The selected statement therefore reflects how complete policy and communication packages are constructed before the public announcement.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a preliminary analysis of the potential effect of reducing the regulatory number of inhabitants per dwelling established in Chile's General Ordinance of Urban Planning and Construction (OGUC) on housing prices. Such a regulatory change would allow a larger number of housing units to be developed on a given land area, giving rise to two opposing mechanisms. On the one hand, a land dilution effect, whereby the cost of land is distributed across a larger number of housing units; on the other hand, a land-value capitalization effect, whereby part of the benefit associated with the increased development capacity is captured by the landowner through an increase in land value. Using a theoretical model and simulation exercises, the analysis shows that the ultimate effect on housing prices depends fundamentally on the extent to which the increase in development capacity is capitalized into land values.

detail.abstract: For a century, management theories disagreed about how organizations should be managed — never about whether the managing agent is human. This paper presents a theoretical framework and an unfolding program of field evidence for a phase transition beyond that premise. In enterprises running on an AI-native operating system, organizations cease to operate as trees of positions and begin to operate as business networks: executable, goal-directed graphs in which humans, AI agents, tools, and data jointly complete work. I name the underlying process Organizational Agency Migration (OAM) — the transfer of organizational agency from human individuals to the socio-technical system across three layers: executive (orchestration), cognitive (organizational learning decoupled from individual learning curves), and teleological (the locus of goal-setting itself). The framework integrates five theoretical moves: a graph-theoretic mechanism (hierarchy as a DAG constrained by human cognitive limits, and its release); organizational memory as an executable, inimitable asset; bidirectional orchestration as the new human–machine constitution; the migration of residual control rights over the objective function as agency theory’s limiting case; and five design principles that succeed the classical principles of unity of command, span of control, and parity of authority and responsibility. The framework is operationalized through preregistered instruments — the CHV curves (capability up, human involvement density down, value per human choice up) and a dual-regime goal-drift discrimination test — within a longitudinal field program of ten enterprises instrumented from before deployment. I theorize the full arc of agency migration; the first observation wave is designed to evidence its onset. Failures will be reported as fully as successes. If the pattern holds, what changes is not merely organizational form but the referent of management theory itself: a candidate third organizational paradigm, in which execution, memory, and eventually candidate ends migrate — and what remains human is choice.
