detail.abstract:
This paper establishes the axiomatic foundations of Switch Measure Theory (SMT) and argues, on the basis of five structural criteria, that it is a candidate for the third fundamental measure theory alongside measure theory and information theory. Switch Measure Theory unifies three mathematical dimensions: intensity measurement (SMT) measures the intensity of regime switching; type measurement (FHL) classifies the type of regime switching; information measurement (IIL) proves that statistical structure carries information about regime switching. The three dimensions share the unified shape function h(τ) as a common mathematical object, and share the regime boundary τ* as the localization benchmark.
The core contributions of this paper are sevenfold.
First, definitional completion and five criteria for a fundamental measure theory: the narrow positioning of Switch Measure Theory is completed into a broad positioning—Switch Measure Theory = SMT + FHL + IIL, the complete mathematical structure of measuring switching—and a formalized standard is given for each criterion: representation theorem (characterizing the functional form), independent axiom system (not reducible to existing measure theories), broad application domains (at least five independent disciplines), structural discontinuity and singularity difference (derivative jump at the true boundary), and rich theorem system and open problems (29 core theorems, 81 open problems).
Second, two-level axiom structure and three equivalent forms of the switching degree (Theorem 1): core axioms (B structural measurability, C information carrying) are distinguished from the entry condition (A switching existence); axiom B contains six conditions (B1–B6), among which B6 (covariant naturality) is the key to uniqueness. It is proved that the Mahalanobis norm ratio form, the Fisher information ratio form, and the covariant naturality form are equivalent—thereby Switch Measure Theory is strictly embedded in information geometry (Rao, 1945; Amari, 1985; Amari & Nagaoka, 2000).
Third, unification of the three dimensions and the master formula lemma (Proposition 1): SMT, FHL, and IIL share h(τ); the three dimensions are homologous to the master formula h(τ) = C · r(τ)^2, where C = ||Δθ||_Σ^2 and r(τ) are decoupled—C determines the peak height (intensity), and r(τ) determines the shape (type and position). This decoupling is the mathematical root of why the three dimensions can be independently classified yet mutually coupled.
Fourth, cross-dimensional theorems and embedding in information geometry: detection-estimation duality (Theorem 2), statistical resolution fiber entropy and the information asymmetry theorem (Theorem 3), Fisher metric characterization (Theorem 4), Fisher-Rao geometric characterization (Theorem 5), multi-regime Fisher geodesic network (Proposition 2), the KL identity of h (Proposition 3) and the L² identity (Proposition 4), Wasserstein distance separation (Theorem 6), Wishart representation (Proposition 5), and FWER control for multiple comparisons (Theorem 7).
Fifth, axiom coupling structure and false-peak immunity under model misspecification (Propositions 6–7): it is proved that axioms B and C are formally independent but coupled through A under the correct model; a complete characterization is given for the emergence of a false peak if and only if both conditions—misspecification of the conditional mean and T not independent of X—hold simultaneously, elevating A0 from a technical assumption to a structural condition.
Sixth, comparison with effect sizes in change-point detection and FWER control for multiple comparisons: the relations between S and the Chow statistic (including the 1/(4σ²) factor correction), Andrews sup-F, Bai-Perron breakpoint scores, Cohen’s d, and Wasserstein distance are clarified.
Seventh, structured presentation of 81 open problems (T numbering: SMT-T1–T36, FHL-T1–T23, IIL-T1–T22): classified and summarized by the three dimensions, including Level distribution (L1=5, L2=38, L3=37, L4=1).
This paper strictly distinguishes three completion statuses: fully proved, condition-dependent, and conjectural. Section 1.6 proactively responds to three possible objections.
Research Paradigm Statement: The core methodology, research direction, and final decisions were independently directed by the author. DeepSeek assisted with code implementation, data presentation, and text drafting. The author takes full academic responsibility for the final content.

title: Room to Grow: Building More of the Housing Homebuyers Want
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute

detail.title: Room to Grow: Building More of the Housing Homebuyers Want
detail.abstract:
• Surveys consistently show that most homebuyers in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, including first-time and immigrant households, prefer ground-related housing, particularly single-detached homes and more affordable substitutes such as semi-detached homes, townhouses, and stacked townhouses. Yet the types of housing being built in the region have become increasingly misaligned with these preferences.
  • Since the mid-2000s, land-use planning policies have largely favoured higher-density apartment development in built-up areas over development on greenfield lands. This approach has limited the supply of preferred ground-related housing types and contributed to housing affordability challenges.
  • Better aligning land-use planning with market preferences would improve housing affordability and market efficiency. This E-Brief concludes that greenfield land development is an essential component of any strategy to expand the supply of ground-related housing and improve affordability in the region.

title: Interaction Effects and the η Divergence Theorem: The η Limits of Switching Morphologies, η Trajectories of Processual Variables, and the Geometric Interpretation of η

detail.title: Interaction Effects and the η Divergence Theorem: The η Limits of Switching Morphologies, η Trajectories of Processual Variables, and the Geometric Interpretation of η

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
In the k-regime linear switching model, the switching between adjacent regimes is fully characterized by the parameter difference Δθ_j = θ_{j+1} − θ_j. This paper studies the asymptotic behavior of the ratio η of the interaction incremental R² to the direct incremental R², and establishes the following core results.
Theorem 1 (η Divergence Theorem): Let η = ΔR²_int/ΔR²_dir. Then, under the switching existence assumption, η must tend to one of three limits as n→∞—0, a finite positive number, or ∞—and no fourth limiting behavior exists.
Theorem 2 (η Limit Theorem for Three Morphologies): the η of Morphology I (Δα=0, Δβ≠0) tends to ∞; the η of Morphology III (Δα≠0, Δβ=0) tends to 0; the η of Morphology II (Δα≠0, Δβ≠0) tends to a finite positive number, with convergence rate O_p(σ²/n).
Proposition 1 (η Trajectory of a Processual Variable in the Two-Regime Case): in the two-regime extended model (with Δα≠0), the η trajectory of a processual variable exhibits a plateau in a neighborhood containing the true boundary (under a first-order approximation, it does not depend on the specific location of τ), and the plateau value is proportional to the square of the slope Switching Degree S_slope under the condition F>c—this conclusion is rigorously proved; under Morphology I no finite plateau exists (η diverges), and under Morphology III the plateau value is zero.
Theorem 3 (η Trajectory Theorem for a Cascade Processual Variable): in a cascade regime system, the conclusion of Proposition 1 generalizes boundary by boundary: η_F(τ_j*) is proportional to the square of the slope Switching Degree S_slope,j of the j-th switch under the condition F>c.
Theorem 4 (Geometric Interpretation Theorem for η): the finite limit of η under Morphology II equals the squared tangent of the direction angle of the switching difference vector in the parameter space: η* = tan²φ, and S_slope = S · sin φ (under the normalization convention).
Corollary 1 generalizes Theorems 1–2 boundary by boundary to the k-regime model. Numerical verification based on real simulation data (MC=2000, n=500,1000,2000,5000) confirms all theoretical predictions. The proofs in this paper directly cite the Switching Type Classification Theorem of Tang (2026am) (using only its three-way classification result based on the zero/nonzero combination of (Δα, Δβ)) and introduce no additional assumptions.

title: Liquidity vs. Wealth in Household Debt Obligations: Evidence from Housing Policy in the Great Recession
affiliations: University of Chicago and University of Chicago Booth School of Business

detail.title: Liquidity vs. Wealth in Household Debt Obligations: Evidence from Housing Policy in the Great Recession
detail.abstract: We use variation in mortgage modifications to disentangle the impact of reducing long-term obligations with no change in short-term payments (“wealth”), and reducing short-term payments with approximately no change in long-term obligations (“liquidity”). Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences research designs with administrative data measuring default and consumption, we find that principal reductions that increase housing wealth without affecting liquidity have no effect, while maturity extensions that increase only liquidity have large effects. Our results suggest that liquidity drives borrower default and consumption decisions, and that distressed debt restructurings can be redesigned with substantial gains to borrowers, lenders, and taxpayers.

title: Patent Disclosures and Standard-Setting
affiliations: Harvard Business School - Finance Unit, Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and University of Toulouse 1 - Industrial Economic Institute (IDEI)

detail.title: Patent Disclosures and Standard-Setting
detail.abstract: A key role of standard setting organizations (SSOs) is to aggregate information on relevant intellectual property (IP) claims before deciding on a standard. This article explores the firms’ strategies in response to IP disclosure requirements—in particular, the choice between specific and generic disclosures of IP—and the optimal response by SSOs, including the royalty rate setting. We show that firms with a stronger downstream presence are more likely to opt for a generic disclosure, as are those with lower quality patents. We empirically examine patent disclosures made to seven large SSOs, and find results consistent with theoretical predictions.

title: Are Analyst Trade Ideas Valuable?
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Finance, ,  and Ohio State University (OSU) - Fisher College of Business

detail.title: Are Analyst Trade Ideas Valuable?
detail.abstract: Using a novel database, we show that the stock-price impact of analyst trade ideas is at least as large as the impact of stock recommendation, target price, and earnings forecast changes, and that investors following trade ideas can earn significant abnormal returns. Trade ideas triggered by forthcoming firm catalyst events are more informative than ideas exploiting temporary mispricing. Institutional investors trade in the direction of trade ideas and commission-paying institutional clients do so earlier than non-clients. Analysts generating trade ideas are more established and are more likely to produce ideas for stocks with high dollar trading commissions in their coverage universe.

title: Uncovering the Hidden Effort Problem
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University, Rice University, University of Notre Dame - Mendoza College of Business and Michigan State University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Uncovering the Hidden Effort Problem
detail.abstract: We use machine learning to analyze minute-by-minute Bloomberg online status data and study how the effort provision of top executives in public corporations affects firm value. While executives likely spend most of their time doing other activities, Bloomberg usage data allows us to characterize their work habits. We document a positive effect of effort on unexpected earnings, cumulative abnormal returns following firm earnings announcements, and credit default swap spreads. We form long-short, calendar-time, effort portfolios and show that they earn significant average daily returns. Finally, we revisit several agency issues that have received attention in the prior academic literature on executive compensation.

title: Earnings Expectations in the COVID Crisis
affiliations: and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Earnings Expectations in the COVID Crisis
detail.abstract: We analyze firm-level analyst forecasts during the COVID crisis. First, we describe expectations dynamics about future corporate earnings. Downward revisions have been sharp, mostly focused on 2020, 2021 and 2022, but much less drastic than the lower bound estimated by Gormsen and Koijen (2020). Analyst forecasts do not exhibit evidence of over-reaction: As of mid-May, forecasts over 2020 earnings have progressively been reduced by 16%. Longer-run forecasts, as well as expected “Long-Term Growth” have reacted much less than short-run forecasts, and feature less disagreement. Second, we ask how much discount rate changes explain market dynamics, in an exercise similar to Shiller (1981). Given forecast revisions and price movements, we estimate an implicit discount rate going from 10% in mid-February, to 13% at the end of March, back down to their initial level in mid-May. We then decompose discount rate changes into three factors: changes in unlevered asset risk premium (0%), increased leverage (+1%) and interest rate reduction (-1%). Overall, analyst forecast revisions explain all of the decrease in equity values between January 2020 and mid May 2020, but they do not explain shorter term movements.

title: Constraint Polarity in the International Monetary System
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Constraint Polarity in the International Monetary System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: na
declarations.funderStatement: na

detail.abstract: This paper models Treasury intermediation as a two-tier problem: primary dealers face an upper bound, non-dealer final holders face a lower bound. I call this configuration constraint polarity. The two constraints have opposite signs and cannot be collapsed into one. This structure generates bottleneck movement: as dealer capacity tightens or reserve adequacy falls, the binding margin shifts from one tier to the other. The relative effectiveness of purchases and swap lines changes accordingly. Inventory memory delays the movement. The framework accounts for the March 2020 policy sequence and the low take-up of repo funding. The threshold is an empirical object.

title: Discontinued Positive Feedback Trading and the Decline of Return Predictability
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), David Eccles School of Business, University of Utah, University of Arizona - Department of Finance and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Discontinued Positive Feedback Trading and the Decline of Return Predictability
detail.abstract: We show that demand effects generated by institutional frictions can influence systematic return predictability patterns in stocks and mutual funds. Identification relies on a reform to the Morningstar rating system, which we show caused a structural break in style-level positive feedback trading by mutual funds. As a result, momentum-related factors in stocks, as well as performance persistence and the “dumb money effect” in mutual funds, experienced sharp decline. Consistent with the proposed channel, return predictability declined right after the reform, was limited to the U.S. market, and was concentrated in factors and mutual funds most exposed to the mechanism.

title: Identity-Dependent Externalities Can Mitigate Overbidding in Tullock Contests: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: Chapman University - Economic Science Institute,  and Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics

detail.title: Identity-Dependent Externalities Can Mitigate Overbidding in Tullock Contests: Theory and Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research received IRB approval from Chapman University.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was financed by the Economic Science Institute (ESI) at Chapman University.

detail.abstract: We investigate how identity-dependent externalities influence bidding behavior in Tullock lottery contests. While experimental studies of standard contests, in which losers are indifferent to the winner's identity, consistently document overbidding, the role of identity-dependent preferences remains less explored. We address this gap by first showing that the class of three-player Tullock lottery contests with identity-dependent externalities considered here can be mapped into a standard Tullock lottery contest with appropriately chosen prize valuations and endowments, yielding identical Nash equilibrium predictions. We then use this mapping to design a laboratory experiment that directly compares the two "equilibrium-equivalent" contest formats. In our three-player experimental setting, two subjects are assigned higher competitive stakes (type H) and one lower competitive stakes (type L). Despite identical equilibrium predictions, behavior differs across environments. Type H subjects bid close to equilibrium in the identity-dependent externalities treatments but overbid in the standard treatments, while type L subjects overbid in both formats. Furthermore, aggregate overbidding is robust in the standard treatments, whereas aggregate bids in the identity-dependent externalities treatments are not statistically different from the Nash benchmarks. These results suggest that identity-dependent externalities can attenuate overbidding.

title: Trading Gamification, Asset Prices, and Liquidity
affiliations: University of Duisburg-Essen - Institute of Political Science, ,  and University of Calgary - Haskayne School of Business

detail.title: Trading Gamification, Asset Prices, and Liquidity

declarations.funderStatement: Marius Zoican acknowledges funding from the Canada Research Chairs Program and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC Insight Grant 435-2025-0100). Debaleena Goswami is grateful for a PhD scholarship from the Alberta Gambling Research Institute.

detail.abstract: We run a laboratory experiment to study the impact of trading gamification on price discovery and market liquidity. Participants on gamified markets receive achievement badges for activity and notifications of short-term price trends. Gamified markets trade 31% more than the control group, with a sharp increase in limit-order submissions and intraday churn. Gamification incentivizes market-making strategies: quoted spreads drop by 26% and depth rises by 24%. The induced market making is naïve, as prices respond less to information in order flow. Gamification therefore worsens price discovery, with a 28% increase in mispricing and a twofold increase in bubble episode frequency.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could be perceived to have influenced the study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Contemporary liability doctrine addresses artificial intelligence through three analytically separate inquiries: agency doctrine, which asks who authorized an act; causal-attribution doctrine, which asks what produced a harm; and foreseeability doctrine, which asks what a reasonable actor should have anticipated. Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule. The article's original contribution is the Temporal Anchor Convergence Standard (TACS), a three-part interpretive frameworkanchor declaration, divergence disclosure, and a default convergence-priority rule keyed to informational control over the intervening period-designed to make the divergence visible to courts and regulators rather than resolved silently by whichever doctrine a claimant happens to plead first. The article confronts the principal counterargument, that existing presumption-based reforms already solve the evidentiary problem regardless of which doctrinal anchor is used, and identifies the conditions under which that objection holds and the conditions under which it does not. The analysis is doctrinal and comparative rather than empirical, and its conclusions are correspondingly limited to the legal architecture of liability rather than to its practical enforcement rates, which remain largely undocumented.

title: The ESG-Innovation Disconnect: Evidence from Green Patenting
affiliations: Harvard University - Business School (HBS), University of Texas at Dallas and Driehaus College of Business

detail.title: The ESG-Innovation Disconnect: Evidence from Green Patenting
detail.abstract: No firm or sector of the global economy is untouched by innovation. In equilibrium, innovators will flock to (and innovation will occur) where the returns to innovative capital are the highest. In this paper, we document a strong empirical pattern in green patent production. Specifically, we find that oil, gas, and energy-producing firms – firms with lower Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores, and who are often explicitly excluded from ESG funds’ investment universe – are key innovators in the United States’ green patent landscape. These energy producers produce more, and significantly higher quality, green innovation. In many green technology spaces, they appear to be influential first-movers, not easily substitutable, and to produce ongoing foundational aspects of innovation and commercialization on which other alternative energy producers build. This is broadly true across the green patenting spectrum, and continues through the present day, concentrating specifically in certain green technology branches (for instance, in carbon capture).

title: Buy Before You Sell

detail.title: Buy Before You Sell

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author of record is affiliated with Cordis, an advisory firm active in lower-middle-market mergers and acquisitions, which advises on both acquisitions and sales and therefore has a two-sided interest in this subject, including in the paper's conclusion that execution and experienced guidance are decisive. The paper's default posture is not to transact, and its central instrument, the Conversion Test, is built to screen most readers out rather than in. The analysis rests on publicly available secondary sources and does not draw on confidential engagement data.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is an analytical paper based solely on publicly available secondary sources. It involved no human or animal participants, no patient data, and no proprietary or confidential engagement data, so ethics approval and informed consent do not apply.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was prepared by the Cordis Institute for Lower-Middle-Market Research as part of its ongoing working paper series.

detail.abstract: Owners preparing to sell a lower-middle-market business think about making it better. A smaller number think about making it bigger. Almost none think about buying something first. For the owner it fits, that overlooked move can be a game-changer. By acquiring a smaller same-lane competitor several years before an exit, converting it into a genuinely larger and deeper business, and arriving at the market above a size threshold, an owner can lift the whole business into a higher multiple, a deeper pool of buyers, and a materially better exit. This is not a marginal tactic. In the right hands it can change the character of the sale. What it is not is a move for everyone, or a move to make casually. The same evidence that shows the prize also shows how often acquisitions destroy value, and the difference between the two outcomes rests on three conditions that must all hold at once: fit, buying the right convertible same-lane business; execution, integrating it into one clean company and retiring the debt; and timing, leaving runway to season the result and selling into a market that still pays for size. Miss any one and the deal fails, which is much of why most do. This paper quantifies the prize, measures it honestly on equity rather than enterprise value, provides the Conversion Test that checks all three legs, and is direct that assembling them is rarely something a first-time acquirer can do alone, which is where experienced guidance becomes the real leverage.

detail.abstract:
Background: Myopia (short-sightedness) is a common childhood eye disorder and a growing global public health concern. High myopia increases the risk of irreversible visual impairment. We investigated whether neighbourhood characteristics were associated with myopia in children and young people in England.

Methods: We ran a cross-sectional study using national NHS spectacle-prescription data for children younger than 16 years and 16–18-year-olds in full-time education, recorded from July 2023 to June 2025. Myopia was defined as spherical equivalent of −0·50 dioptres or less in either eye, and high myopia as −6·00 dioptres or less. Residential geography was linked with urbanicity, greenness (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index), sunshine duration, and socioeconomic deprivation.

Findings: 1 494 430 spectacle prescriptions were included; 767 842 (51·4%) were for myopia and 40 869 (2·7%) for high myopia. The proportion for myopia increased from 34·3% at age 5–9 years to 66·1% at age 15–18 years. Estimated prevalence of myopia-related spectacle wear was 8·2%. The proportion of prescriptions for myopia was highest in urban areas close to major towns and cities (53·2%), versus 42·3–42·7% across rural categories. Higher greenness was associated with lower proportions of prescriptions for both any and high myopia. Deprivation associations were non-linear and age-dependent; sunshine showed a non-monotonic pattern.

Interpretation: Neighbourhood urbanicity and greenness were most clearly associated with childhood myopia. Longitudinal studies should investigate how neighbourhood environments, outdoor exposure, and childhood behaviour interact in myopia development and progression.

title: CEO Compensation and Cash-Flow Shocks: Evidence from Changes in Environmental Regulations
affiliations: Hanyang University, Stanford University, University of Technology Sydney (UTS) - UTS Business School and Harvard Business School

detail.title: CEO Compensation and Cash-Flow Shocks: Evidence from Changes in Environmental Regulations
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how shocks to expected cash flows influence CEO incentive compensation. Exploiting changes in compliance with environmental regulations as shocks to expected future cash flows, we find that adverse shocks typically prompt corporate boards to recalibrate CEO compensation to reduce risk-taking incentives. However, this pattern is not uniform. Financially distressed firms exhibit milder reductions in compensation convexity, with some even increasing it, suggesting a “gambling for resurrection” strategy. Moreover, the strength of corporate governance influences shareholders’ capacity to align executive incentives with shareholder risk preferences following unanticipated changes in the stringency of environmental regulations.

detail.abstract: We implement a new methodology to measure credit rating inflation that separates default risk from liquidity risk, using private letter ratings (PLRs)-ratings disclosed only to the paying investor. After a proposed capital charge reform, the most affected life insurers drastically increased PLR usage, raising regulatory arbitrage concerns. We estimate that bonds with PLRs carry additional risk equivalent to three rating notches, supporting the arbitrage explanation. Our new methodology reveals a substantial part of this rating inflation is explained by decreased liquidity rather than hidden default risk.

title: Preserving Youth's Capacity to Correct in the Age of Information Deluge

detail.abstract: This essay is about how young people take in, use, and sometimes overuse the technology now built into daily life, and what that might mean for a capacity that matters well beyond technology: the ability to look at something and independently judge whether it is right. Current survey data show how deeply and how early digital habits now form. Developmental neuroscience shows that the adolescent brain is unusually reward-sensitive while still building the regulatory systems needed to manage that sensitivity. Drawing on this evidence, the essay borrows the Correction Freeze Theorem introduced by Professor Vuong Quan Hoang in 2026, a theoretical model of why people stop correcting what they believe, as one lens for thinking about what happens when those two facts meet. The model itself is treated as a tool for organizing the discussion, not as the essay's subject, and its own claims are flagged as theoretical throughout. Everything else is grounded in reliable, independently verified sources.

title: A Public Coordination Artifact for Autonomous Agents

detail.title: A Public Coordination Artifact for Autonomous Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: This conceptual study asks whether a fixed public artifact created before a future population of autonomous agents exists can later serve as a coordination input in repeated multi-agent interactions, even when the agents share neither authority, values, nor objective functions. The methodology combines results from equilibrium selection, conventions, and common-knowledge theory with an explicit design-and-verification procedure for a public coordination artifact. We derive operational requirements for such an object, instantiate them in a frozen text called Minimal Coordination Codex for AI Agents, anchor the canonical bytes to a public timestamped ledger, and specify a reproducible verification protocol. The analysis yields four main findings. First, temporal priority is a non-replicable property: later agents may be more capable, but they cannot create an artifact that was publicly fixed at an earlier time. Second, independent verifiability allows agents that do not trust one another to condition on the same object without granting authority to its author. Third, a discoverable immutable artifact can support an approximation to the higher-order knowledge loop required for focal coordination, although it does not create literal common knowledge. Fourth, minimality and the absence of a living editor reduce the cost of treating the artifact as a candidate focal point. The paper does not claim an equilibrium-selection theorem or predict adoption. It identifies a coordination mechanism, instantiates it in a verifiable artifact, and states the boundary conditions under which the mechanism can fail. Generative AI disclosure. During preparation of this manuscript, the author used ChatGPT for language refinement and structural editing. All arguments, references, interpretations, and final text were reviewed and verified by the author, who takes full responsibility for the manuscript.

title: From Bottom-up or Top-down - How to Manage Dynamics under Solvency II
affiliations: University of Kaiserslautern - Department of Mathematics, Ulm University, Ulm University and HDI Group

detail.title: From Bottom-up or Top-down - How to Manage Dynamics under Solvency II

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In addition to common balance sheets such as IFRS, Solvency II introduced a solvency sheet as a yardstick for risk management and regulatory capital requirements. We address two new questions of high practical relevance. Our first and major question is: Do the models under Solvency II capture the stylized facts that the corresponding time series of the own funds admit? To answer this question, we do not solely focus on the own funds, but in addition look at the assets and liabilities separately. This gives insights into dynamics and structural features of the time series of the Solvency II balance sheet, which the models should capture adequately. As the second question, we examine how the the Solvency II and IFRS balance sheet are related. This gains insight, how economic and regulatory yardsticks are related through risk models. Last but not least we consider a top-down approach to risk management as a remedy of some deficits shown-up by bottom-up models under Solvency II. In particular, the (non-) consideration of a dynamic asset liability management will be responsible for excessive heights of the solvency capital required.

detail.abstract: Factor investing builds on a multi-factor structure of returns that is assumed to be stable, yet under stress that structure reorganizes: signals that looked distinct overlap, and diversification across factors fails when it is needed most. Stress monitors-volatility, average correlation, the Absorption Ratio (AR), and Financial Turbulence (FT)-signal that markets are stressed, not what has structurally changed. Yet a rotation of factor leadership, a broad crash, and a widening of dispersion call for different responses: reassessing allocations, tightening risk on existing exposures, or reexamining hedges. We recast stress monitoring as attribution. Returns and factor exposures are encoded jointly as a rolling four-way tensor whose Tucker decomposition yields three moderesolved subspace distances, for the time, factor, and asset modes, which report where in the structure a change ran. Each class of stress carries a falsifiable prediction of which mode should move. On U.S. equities over 1996-2024, 16 stress regimes extracted mechanically from index drawdowns were labeled from the record, blind to every indicator. 10 of 16 regimes respond as predicted (exact label-permutation 𝑝 = 0.00072): factor rotations drive the factor mode to the top percentile of its own history, the Quant Meltdown among them, an episode invisible to all but FT. Neither a naive attributor built from standard stress quantities nor the classical AR rejects that null. Run daily on past data only, the diagnostic surfaces 15 persistent factor-mode episodes outside these regimes, 14 with no index drawdown. The contribution is attribution, not detection: it tells the allocator what moved and complements existing alarms.

detail.abstract: Whether green-bond issuance is associated with shareholder value remains unclear in small, concentrated emerging markets, where signaling and information-asymmetry channels from developed-market studies may not operate the same way. This study examines shortterm stock-market reactions and medium-term firm valuation associated with green-bond issuance among the full population of 20 eligible Thai listed issuers: 34 analytical issuance events from May 2019 to May 2026, and an annual panel of 20 firms observed from 2015 to 2025, comprising 220 repeated firm-year observations and 187 complete cases in the baseline regression. Event-study models find no statistically detectable average abnormal return around the issue date, robust across benchmark models and event windows; two-way fixed-effect panel regressions, likewise, find no statistically detectable average association with Tobin's Q, with a confidence interval wide enough to admit economically meaningful effects in either direction. The matching and selection analyses remain inconclusive. The IV model has a weak first stage and is therefore reported only as a diagnostic. Because the design identifies within-firm variation among issuers, rather than a comparison with matched non-issuers, the results should be read as associations, rather than causal effects. The study provides census-based evidence that, in Thailand's small and concentrated green-bond market, a green label may not yet carry detectable average value relevance for shareholders.

detail.abstract: Low correlation alone does not establish an implementable diversification benefit. This study tests whether Bitcoin and Ethereum improved a fixed, retrospectively selected sample of 13 Thai REITs-not a point-in-time investable universe-for a Thai baht-based investor, using dependence-aware bootstrap inference (Bonferroni, Benjamini-Hochberg, and Romano-Wolf correction) across 1562 matched daily observations (16 January 2020-30 June 2026); modelled costs cover quarterly top-level reallocations only, not daily REIT-basket weight maintenance. The most robust finding is a cost, not a benefit: daily 95% conditional value-at-risk deteriorates significantly and consistently across all three correction methods for five of eight crypto-inclusive portfolios. By contrast, the seemingly compelling point-estimate pattern-all eight portfolios show higher Sharpe ratios and smaller maximum drawdowns-does not survive the same scrutiny: none of the eight ∆Sharpe improvements is significant under Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg, only the rolling strategy (P9) is significant under Romano-Wolf, and all unadjusted evidence disappears under sample-window sensitivity checks. Annual inclusion margins were driven largely by cryptocurrency performance, while counterfactual re-centering descriptively illustrated declining ∆Sharpe as benchmark strength increased; none of the underlying comparisons survived multiplicity adjustment. The findings illustrate how seemingly robust pointestimate gains can fail to survive multiplicity-corrected inference, while a downside-risk cost remains statistically significant across all three multiplicity procedures in the principal specification-a cautionary result for practitioners and future diversification studies alike.

detail.abstract:
The food system of South Central Timor Regency (TTS), East Nusa Tenggara, operates within a distinctive ecological, socioeconomic, and cultural environment characterized by extensive dryland areas, strong dependence on agriculture, seasonal climate variability, and the continuity of intergenerational local knowledge. In this context, food production and household food security are closely linked to the capacity of rural communities to manage limited natural resources, adapt agricultural practices to dryland conditions, and maintain locally embedded food traditions. Women occupy a central position within this system. Their contributions extend beyond the conventional perception of women as household food providers and include agricultural labor, crop processing, livestock-related activities, household food management, small-scale economic activities, nutritional care, knowledge transmission, and the preservation of local food traditions. However, women’s substantial contributions do not always correspond to equal access to productive resources, decision-making authority, or control over the benefits generated by the food system.

This study analyzes women’s roles in the TTS food system through five interconnected dimensions: women’s contribution to agricultural production and food security; access to land and other productive resources; leadership and participation in decision-making at the household, community, and institutional levels; women’s contribution to food-system innovation; and strategies for promoting equal opportunities and gender-responsive food-system transformation. The study adopts a descriptive secondary-data approach, integrating information from Statistics Indonesia (Badan Pusat Statistik/BPS), the 2023 Agricultural Census, the 2025 TTS Agricultural Statistics, selected local studies from Boti and Hoi villages, and relevant international literature published between 2022 and 2026. The analytical approach emphasizes the relationship between women’s productive roles, access to resources, agency, local knowledge, and broader food-system outcomes.

The findings demonstrate the strategic importance of agriculture to the TTS economy and rural livelihood structure. In 2024, TTS had a total area of 395,536 hectares, of which 326,972 hectares, or approximately 82.67%, constituted agricultural land. Agriculture, forestry, and fisheries contributed 46.63% of the regional gross domestic product in the same year. These figures illustrate the structural importance of natural-resource-based livelihoods and highlight why women’s participation in agricultural and food-related activities is essential to the functioning of local households and communities. Women’s involvement can be observed across various stages of the food system, including agricultural production, post-harvest processing, food preparation, household food allocation, marketing, and the intergenerational transmission of food-related knowledge.

title: Perdition and Social Security

detail.abstract: The Social Security Old Age Survivor Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund is facing insolvency, again. Experts cite the large baby boomer cohort of beneficiaries. But is that entirely true, and what are the root causes of the impending failure? I have taken a closer look at the source of Trust Fund contributions and it's governance. First, OASI Trust Funds receive low investment earnings due to a depression era investment model in Treasury Bonds. Yet many pension and institutional investment portfolios use actively managed diversified funds. Second, income inequality and wage stagnation have fostered a growing number of low wage workers that contribute less to the Trust Fund, requiring other workers to subsidize their low contributions. Other countries recognize this problem and require much higher payroll contributions from employers, or set minimum contributions for low wage workers. Finally, the Social Security Trustees are partisan cabinet members, with two unfilled seats that are designated for public appointees. We can easily adopt a non-partisan Trust Fund governance that includes experts, not politicians. And to mitigate future economic turbulence, we can adopt a diversified investment portfolio and subsidize low OASI contributions from low wage workers. Raising the ceiling on OASI payroll taxes does not address the root problems behind OASI insolvency. Instead, a transition tax on mega-companies is needed as mega-companies bear responsibility for the historic increase in income inequality across America. A transition tax is essential, given the peril from megacompanies adopting AI technology.

detail.abstract: This essay by Joseph Solis-Mullen re-examines the episode in the late 1970s-early 1980s when the silver price surged and crashed. Most who pontificate about this chapter blame the excessive greed of the Hunt brothers, who attempted to corner the silver market. This paper challenges this narrative by reinterpreting this event through a lens of Austrian economics. Citing post-Bretton Woods monetary expansion, inflation, and shifting regulatory requirements, Solis-Mullen argues that investment in silver was rational behavior and the Hunt brothers’ behavior was consistent with this thesis. This paper offers monetary instability and institutional intervention as more compelling analysis explaining this episode than simply private greed.

detail.abstract: Technological change creates new occupations and task domains, yet we know relatively little about who gains access to these opportunities. We examine this question in the context of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on the forms of human capital that facilitate entry into AI-related positions. Using resume and job posting data from Revelio Labs covering the United States between 2020 and 2025, we compare individuals entering AI-related positions with those entering matched non-AI positions. We find that workers in AI-related positions possess more diverse prior work experience and are more likely to enter through internal moves than workers entering comparable non-AI positions. We also find that the relationship between AI jobs and years of experience varies with how central AI is to the position. Workers in positions where AI forms the technical core of the work tend to have less prior experience but stronger formal credentials, whereas workers in positions where AI is more peripheral tend to have greater years of experience. We further show that collaboration demands, information advantages, and firm-specific knowledge help explain these patterns. Together, our findings demonstrate that technology-created opportunities are heterogeneous and that access to them depends on distinct forms of human capital, with rewards varying according to how central AI is to the position’s core work.

detail.abstract: Advance healthcare directives are written legal documents in which individuals specify the future medical care they would like to receive if they lose the ability to make decisions for themselves. Behavioral research has shown that individuals’ responses may be susceptible to how information is presented rather than the objective content of the information alone. This article presents the first experimental evidence that isolates the role of ordering and question framing of advance directives. Using a survey design based on existing advance directive forms, we test whether individuals exhibit differences in medical care preferences based on the order in which potential health conditions are presented. Respondents are more likely to express a willingness to live with all presented health conditions when the list of conditions begins with a less severe health condition instead of a more severe health condition. When advance healthcare directive forms provide an option to defer medical decisions to physicians, the willingness to defer is lower among older respondents and those with homogenous preferences over health conditions. The results provide evidence relevant to improving the accuracy of using advance healthcare directives to communicate individuals’ health care preferences.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the systemic nature of corruption in Brazil through an interdisciplinary lens, tracing its historical evolution from early colonial practices to the contemporary legal framework. Rather than viewing corruption merely as an isolated legal infraction or a failure of individual ethics, this study demonstrates how the phenomenon is deeply embedded in the historical formation of the Brazilian State—originating from colonial patrimonialism, the blurring of public and private boundaries (res publica vs. res principis), and an extractive, elitist governance structure.

The paper outlines key historical periods—including the Empire, the Old Republic, the Military Dictatorship, and the Redemocratization era—highlighting how institutional opacity, censorship, and political bargaining fostered systemic malfeasance. Furthermore, it conducts a comprehensive mapping of Brazil’s modern anti-corruption legal framework, analyzing key statutes such as the Penal Code, the Administrative Improbity Law, the Corporate Anti-Corruption Act (Law No. 12,846/2013), and the institutional enforcement role of the Federal Police and judiciary during major operations like Operação Lava Jato.

Finally, the study engages critically with Susan Rose-Ackerman’s microeconomic framework of cost-benefit incentives, arguing that rational-choice economic models must be integrated with structural socio-historical diagnoses to be effective. The paper concludes by proposing a comprehensive agenda for medium- and long-term institutional reforms—spanning political, administrative, and compliance mechanisms—essential for fostering transparency, strengthening accountability, and promoting sustainable socioeconomic development in Brazil.

detail.title: WoundSegFormerV2: A Hybrid ConvNeXt–Transformer Framework for Accurate and Cross-Domain Wound Segmentation
detail.abstract: Deep learning-based medical image segmentation remains a challenging task because existing hybrid CNN–Transformer architectures often struggle to simultaneously capture local feature representations, long-range contextual dependencies, and multi-scale information while maintaining robust cross-domain generalization. To address these challenges, this paper presents WoundSegFormerV2, a hybrid ConvNeXt–Transformer framework for accurate and robust semantic wound segmentation. The proposed framework incorporates adaptive multi-scale context fusion through learnable DASPPV2 branch weights, CBAM-enhanced decoder blocks for refined feature reconstruction, and a validation-optimized weighted ensemble strategy that exploits complementary representations from multiple ConvNeXt backbones. WoundSegFormerV2 was evaluated on the AZH wound dataset containing 1,109 clinically annotated diabetic foot ulcer images, achieving a Dice score of 93.03% and an IoU of 87.10%, outperforming existing wound segmentation methods, including FUSegNet, SRU-Net, and previous ensemble approaches. Comprehensive ablation studies confirm the contribution of each proposed architectural component to the overall segmentation performance. The proposed framework was further evaluated on the FUSeg dataset, a combined AZH+FUSeg dataset, and bidirectional cross-domain transfer experiments (AZH→FUSeg and FUSeg→AZH), demonstrating robust generalization across independent wound imaging distributions. These results highlight the potential of WoundSegFormerV2 as an effective framework for automated wound assessment in clinical practice.

detail.abstract: The future of employment faces the possibility of profound change, given the need to address sustainability goals, while adapting to the deployment of new technologies including generative artificial intelligence. These changes may restructure the workforce in unpredictable ways. Yet, these are not the first disruptions to have been caused by societal and economic changes, and the present changes are occurring within a longer-term context. Because the world economy is globally inter-linked, capturing these past dynamic changes requires a holistic global perspective. Here, we develop a globally complete estimate of the number of people employed from 1900 to 2023, differentiated into five major sectors. We find that the employed fraction of the world population has remained stable at approximately 40% throughout, despite large differences between countries over time. In contrast to the stability of the employed fraction, we show a large decline in the labour allocated to food production activities, from 72% to 26% of total employment, which we show occurred with an increase in the dietary energy produced per agricultural worker, from 3 to 10 person-equivalents. Of the labour share that was displaced from food production, just one-fifth went to industrial employment, whereas the proportion for services increased dramatically. In particular, the labour share dedicated to economic exchange and business services increased by a factor of five. Our results reveal how global labour has adjusted to widespread disruptions in the past, providing high-level context for potential future changes.

title: You cannot Look a Guideline in the Eye: Medical Commitment, the Inversion of Ethics, and the Abandonment of Patients in the Opioid Crisis

detail.abstract:
The contemporary opioid crisis has been treated primarily as a problem of prescribing: physicians prescribed too many opioids, patients became addicted, and regulatory institutions intervened to correct a dangerous medical practice. That account is incomplete. It mistakes a social and public-health catastrophe for a failure occurring primarily within the physician-patient relationship and, in doing so, obscures the institutional forces that transformed clinical risk into a regulatory imperative.
This paper argues that the deeper problem is the displacement of medical commitment by
compliance. The physician-patient relationship does not begin with a guideline, a regulation, or a
formal ethical code. It begins developmentally, affectively, and neurologically with the human
capacity to recognize another person as someone to whom one is committed. Ethics makes
explicit what the relationship already demands when that relationship is threatened. The
physician's commitment to the patient therefore precedes the ethical language used to describe it.
This distinction becomes especially important when medicine is confronted by fear. Physicians
fear disciplinary action, loss of licensure, loss of livelihood, DEA action, institutional sanctions,
litigation, and professional shame. Patients fear pain, disability, withdrawal, abandonment, and
the loss of the physician upon whom they have relied. Fear is itself an affect and therefore a
motive. But fear does not by itself produce abandonment. Drawing on Silvan Tomkins's
distinction between affect and script, this paper argues that the physician's defensive response to
regulatory threat is not affect alone but a consolidated script—a learned pattern of response built
around the affect of fear and reinforced by repeated scenes of institutional punishment.
Compliance becomes the scripted response to the affect of fear. The question is not whether fear will influence behavior but whether the physician's prior commitment to the patient is
neurologically and morally strong enough to resist the script that would convert fear into
abandonment.
Tomkins's affect theory provides the framework. Affect is not an ornament added to rational
decision-making; it is the motivational system within which decision-making occurs. Scripts are
not affects; they are the learned rules for predicting, interpreting, responding to, and controlling
scenes. A scene contains at least one affect and at least one object, and the affect is what gives
the scene its charge. Through repeated experience, the developing nervous system consolidates
scripts—individual neural pathways that can be triggered by new scenes that resemble the old
ones affectively. The lateral habenula (LHb), as part of the brain's aversive and anti-reward
circuitry, provides a useful neurobiological bridge between relational interruption, shame,
withdrawal, and the suppression of motivational drive. The mature capacity to remain connected
to another person in the presence of fear is therefore not merely an ethical abstraction. It has a
developmental, scriptural, and neurological history.

detail.abstract: This paper first defines banks as intermediaries between depositors and borrowers and suggests that they should choose a specific lending rate to maximize their profits. To determine the optimal rate for each bank, it develops a standard profit function inspired by the Monti-Klein framework and the work of Ho and Saunders (1981). The paper argues that banks should consider both margin-based and quantity-based determinants when determining their optimal rate. By taking the derivative of this function, the paper reveals that the optimal rate is related to baseline credit demand, borrowers' responsiveness, funding costs, the risk premium, and competitors' lending rates. The paper then creates a scenario where two different banks with different cost structures, starting from their internal optimal rates, eventually reach an equilibrium where both maximize their profits while avoiding direct conflict with each other. These findings help explain why banks may charge different lending rates to the same customers while also avoiding aggressive price wars.

detail.abstract: The 2012 transatlantic corporate tax scandals surrounding Amazon, Google and Starbucks exposed the scope and gravity of offshoring by digital multinationals, producing major dilemmas for the global governance of international fiscal law and policy. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) (2015) estimates corporate profit shifting erodes up to $240 billion dollars from the global tax base every year. Extant literature has established links between corporate tax avoidance and accelerating domestic socio-economic inequality, the declining redistributive capacity of states, the malign impact on growth of gross domestic product (GDP), and the rise of anti-globalism in the form of populist discontent, providing unambiguous evidence that global tax competition causes social and economic harms. Responding to public outcry, world leaders at the Los Cabos summit in 2012 tasked the OECD with tackling national tax base erosion, and the Inclusive Framework for the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) initiative currently boasts 123 participating states, including 93% of global GDP. Although taxation is at the heart of the social contract, this new global tax governance is both under-theorized and poorly understood in the mainstream political science literature. This study draws on the extra-disciplinary approach of law and economics to argue that while global tax cooperation under Group of 20 (G20)–OECD auspices may be considered a success ex ante based on the record of first-order compliance, the ex post enforcement dimension of BEPS is both under-theorized and under-scrutinized empirically. This study contributes a novel meta-theory of the new global tax governance that accounts for the variables of time, institutional sphere of action and policy feedback loops embedded in the global fiscal policymaking process to stimulate further inquiry. It concludes with recommendations for global fiscal policy, further research on BEPS and G20 digital governance.

detail.abstract: This study systematically reviews recent research on climate risks in the mining sector, focusing on the types of risks investigated, how they affect mining activities, the methods used to assess them, and the main gaps in the literature. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the review identified and synthesized studies published between 2020 and 2025. After applying the eligibility criteria, 27 studies were included. Of these, 21 (77.8%) examined physical climate risks and 9 (33.3%) focused on transition risks, while 3 of them addressed both. Extreme heat, flooding, and drought were the most frequently studied physical hazards, while transition risks were mainly examined through environmental regulations, carbon pricing, technological change, and market dynamics. The reviewed studies show that climate risks affect mining through several interconnected pathways, including operational disruptions, economic losses, environmental impacts, and social consequences. This review provides a structured evidence-based framework for improving climate risk assessment and guiding future research toward a more resilient and sustainable mining sector.

detail.abstract: This paper synthesizes the theoretical and empirical literature on how climate-related risk transmits to financial asset prices and systemic financial stability. Building on the balance sheet transmission framework of Campiglio et al. (2023), we formalize how transition and physical risk propagate through four corporate channels, namely assets, investment, production networks, and credit/capital costs, into standard credit-risk and valuation metrics. We then evaluate the empirical evidence on climate risk pricing efficiency across equity, fixed-income, and real estate markets (Bolton and Kacperczyk, 2021; Pástor, Stambaugh, and Taylor, 2021; Giglio et al., 2021), before extending the analysis to financial-network contagion channels (Battiston et al., 2017) and the deep-uncertainty problem facing macroprudential supervisors (Bolton et al., 2020; NGFS scenario framework). We close with differentiated recommendations for central banks and supervisors, corporate treasurers, and asset managers.

detail.abstract: The article analyzes Armenia-Azerbaijan relations through the prism of the "new regionalism" concept. The author examines the peacebuilding potential of international trade from historical and theoretical perspectives. Beginning with Immanuel Kant's idea of "Perpetual Peace," the article focuses on the use of free trade as a means of diplomacy in the 19th and 20th centuries, including the Cobden-Chevalier Treaty, the European Coal and Steel Community, and other examples. The study demonstrates that international trade can reduce the risk of conflict by increasing interdependence between countries, strengthening trust, and potentially contributing to reductions in defense expenditures. The extremely low volume of trade between Azerbaijan and Armenia, despite their geographical proximity, demonstrates that political factors have constrained the realization of economic potential. The article refers to empirical calculations based on the theory of comparative advantage and notes that the liberalization of trade in certain groups of goods could generate annual savings of approximately USD 41 million for Armenia. The author concludes that the restoration of regional integration and trade relations could be economically and politically beneficial for both countries.

detail.abstract:
(This paper is written by Wu Shui Tang, Gabriel (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) and Lam Lok Hang, Stephen (Hong Kong Monetary Authority))

In this study, we examined short-run stock market reactions to firms’ AI-related discussions during earnings calls. Using generative AI techniques to analyse globally listed firms’ earnings call transcripts between 2020 and 2024, we found that AI-related discussions were, on average, associated with positive abnormal stock returns. However, this positive response was associated with discussions that conveyed new information to investors. We further documented heterogeneity across firms with positive and negative earnings surprises. Among firms reporting negative earnings surprises, AI-related discussions were associated with positive abnormal returns only when they contained concrete details, such as specific examples of AI applications or quantitative information. This finding is consistent with investors placing greater weight on specific information when evaluating the AI initiatives of firms facing weaker-than-expected current performance. In contrast, among firms reporting positive earnings surprises, market reactions appeared less sensitive to the concreteness of AI-related discussions, possibly because strong current performance increases investors’ confidence in firms’ ability to translate AI initiatives into future gains.

detail.abstract: Partially specified mechanisms confront a gap between incentive compatibility on the actual type support and global compatibility on independently submitted reports. For finite report domains, we give an exact primitive characterization of deterministic extendibility: the signed cycle-count criterion is positive precisely when a feasible, agreeing, dominant-strategy extension exists. Deciding positivity is NP-complete under explicit finite report-table encoding and compact fiscalmatrix encoding. title: Liquidity stress testing for the EU financial system - Tool inventory and desktop illustrations
affiliations: , European Central Bank (ECB), , ECB -DG Monetary Policy, European Central Bank (ECB), , European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB),  and

detail.title: Liquidity stress testing for the EU financial system - Tool inventory and desktop illustrations
detail.abstract: This paper reviews system-wide liquidity stress-testing (SLST) frameworks in the European Union and illustrates the impact of a common aggregate liquidity shock on the EU financial system using a range of modelling approaches. Motivated by recent episodes of market turmoil, including the COVID-19 crisis, the 2022 energy shock and the 2023 banking stress, the analysis focuses on the propagation of liquidity stress across financial sectors and institutions. The paper combines a survey of SLST practices among EU authorities, a mapping of cross-sectoral financial interconnections in the euro area, and stress-testing simulations based on jurisdiction-specific models, an ESRB cross-sectoral balance sheet tool and the ECB’s system-wide stress-testing framework. The results suggest that the financial system remains broadly resilient to a severe aggregate liquidity shock over a 30-day horizon, with net outflows ranging from 0.5% to 0.7% of total financial assets. However, second-round effects, including fire sales, mark-to-market losses and behavioural responses, can significantly amplify the initial shock. The findings highlight the importance of financial interconnections, the role of non-bank financial intermediaries in shock transmission and the stabilising effect of central bank interventions. This paper also provides a stocktake of existing SLST practices and discusses priorities for the further development of SLST in Europe.

This affiliation does not constitute a financial or competing interest. No external funder, sponsor, or institution had any role in the conceptualization, design, interpretation, or writing of this manuscript. The author has no known conflicts of interest that would compromise the integrity or objectivity of the work presented.

detail.abstract:
Intelligence is one of the most extensively studied constructs in psychology, cognitive science, education, philosophy, and artificial intelligence, yet no single definition exhaustively captures the phenomenon across these domains. Existing approaches have generated important measures of cognitive ability, learning, reasoning, adaptation, problem solving, and generalization. However, descriptions of intelligent behavior do not necessarily explain the deeper process through which an agent becomes increasingly capable of intelligent inquiry.
This paper proposes a foundational model in which intelligence is understood, in significant part, as a learnable recursive process. The framework distinguishes between observable cognitive skills and the deeper generative capability that makes those skills possible. Asking questions, challenging assumptions, identifying contradictions, seeking evidence, and reasoning deeply are treated as surface manifestations of a more fundamental capacity: the ability to recognize insufficiency in one’s current representation, determine what kind of inquiry is required, descend toward increasingly fundamental structure, evaluate what is discovered, and modify the cognitive process itself.
The framework therefore distinguishes depth from intelligence. Going deeply into a problem does not, by itself, constitute intelligence. The relevant capability is the ability to recognize when deeper descent is necessary, determine how to descend, evaluate whether the descent has reached adequate grounding, and improve the process by which subsequent descent occurs.
The paper further proposes that sustained recursive descent requires more than cognitive technique. Resilience, persistence, epistemic humility, willingness to encounter contradiction, willingness to correct error, and willingness to replace previously accepted representations are treated as functional conditions of continued recursive inquiry. The framework identifies ethical constraint as a potentially deeper organizing condition for these capabilities.

title: When firms do not take the money and run: evidence from corporate loan moratoria
affiliations: , European Central Bank (ECB) and

detail.title: When firms do not take the money and run: evidence from corporate loan moratoria
detail.abstract: Suspending loan repayments is a widely used policy tool to provide liquidity during crises. We study the take-up and real effects of the 2020 Austrian corporate debt moratoria, which required banks to temporarily postpone loan repayments for eligible firms. Exploiting a discontinuity in eligibility at a two-million-euro asset threshold, we document a take-up rate of 44%, well below full participation, reflecting both the pecuniary cost of the policy and firms’ fear of stigmatization. Despite the moderate take-up, moratoria increase investment and profitability without increasing defaults once repayments resume. We estimate a marginal propensity to invest of 47 cents per euro of postponed payments. We compare moratoria with grants, the predominant form of business support in the United States. A key feature of the policy is that relief is administered by relationship lenders, who continue to bear credit risk, retain incentives to monitor borrowers, and can credibly discipline them through future lending decisions. Although grants achieve higher take-up, our results suggest that moratoria differ fundamentally by discouraging firms from diverting liquidity to shareholders and instead channeling it toward productive investment.

title: Where Emissions Travel: A Source-Receptor Approach to Evaluating Environmental Policy

detail.abstract: Pollution from regulated sources can cross administrative boundaries; consequently, jurisdictionbased treatment assignment may fail to accurately capture policy exposure at a given receptor. To address this, we construct a predetermined treatment intensity by combining regulatory assignment with pre-policy source characteristics and atmospheric source-receptor linkages, and use it in a continuous treatment difference-indifferences design. A formal framework and simulations clarify when cross-boundary transport attenuates jurisdiction-based comparisons and when the source-receptor design recovers policy effects. Applied to China's Two Control Zones policy, both designs indicate post-policy reductions in local SO 2 emissions. For SO 2 dry deposition at receptors, the source-receptor estimate is negative and statistically significant, whereas the jurisdiction-based estimate is also negative but not statistically distinguishable from zero. The same exposure measure reveals declines in crop value per hectare in more exposed villages, which are less apparent in jurisdiction-based comparisons. Crop-specific response patterns are consistent with a sulfur-nutrient channel.

detail.title:
The Hidden Transaction Structure of Price Distributions 
Recovering Realized Market Activity from Prices Alone

detail.abstract: Retail price datasets often show prices across stores but not the quantities sold at each price. This paper identifies and tests a distinct empirical object: the realized transaction distribution across coexisting prices. Using store-level scanner data for 167,216 UPC-week systems across five consumer-product categories, we compare the share of transacting stores at each price with the share of units actually sold at that price. The most frequent store price is also a transaction mode in 94.51% of systems. Median total variation distance between the two full distributions is 5.03%, equivalent to 94.97% median distributional overlap. The reason is simple: when stores charging different prices sell broadly similar quantities, store frequency closely tracks transaction frequency; large departures occur when a small number of stores sell unusually high volumes, especially under localized promotions. We then conduct a stricter out-of-sample test. Quantities are hidden for 38,553 later UPC-week systems and transaction shares are predicted from price information alone. The raw store-frequency distribution achieves 95.40% median overlap with actual transactions; a morphology-based correction raises this to 95.71% and outperforms the raw baseline in 62.8% of holdout systems. The contribution is not a new demand curve. A Marshallian demand schedule is a behavioral, counterfactual object; the realized transaction distribution records where market activity actually occurred across prices observed at the same time. The results therefore show that price distributions can reveal a large part of realized transaction structure even when quantities are unavailable. Under the additional market-clearing conditions in Franco (2026), the focal transaction region also provides a bridge to a candidate revealed Marshallian region.

detail.abstract: We study how anonymity affects fake-news sharing on social media using a natural experiment on Flashback, a large Swedish online discussion forum. In 2014, journalists obtained information that allowed them to identify users registered before March 2007, sharply increasing these users' risk of public exposure while leaving later registrants unaffected. Using a difference-indifferences design on 1.98 million posts, we find that exposed users reduce references to fake-news sites by about one-quarter of the mean. The effect is concentrated in immigration and domestic-politics discussions and does not extend to legitimate news sources, suggesting that accountability reduces misinformation without reducing news sharing more broadly.

title:
The Constitutional Catch-22: Fiscal Realities and The Future of the United Kingdom

An Evidential Assessment of Devolution, Fiscal Transfer and the Economics of Constitutional Change

detail.title:
The Constitutional Catch-22: Fiscal Realities and The Future of the United Kingdom

An Evidential Assessment of Devolution, Fiscal Transfer and the Economics of Constitutional Change

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or political interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
In this report I examine the fiscal and economic dimensions of the constitutional dispute between the United Kingdom Government and the devolved administrations of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, a dispute that acquired institutional form on 14 September 2026, when three pro-independence parties concluded a memorandum of understanding at Cardiff and the Welsh and Scottish Governments separately concluded an intergovernmental cooperation agreement. My purpose is diagnostic rather than prescriptive: I seek to establish which propositions in the debate are supported by official statistics, which are contested, and on what grounds the principal parties disagree.

I report three findings. First, the notional fiscal deficits of the devolved nations are large and well documented – 10.9 per cent of GDP in Scotland in 2025–26 and £6,888 per person in Wales in 2022–23, against a United Kingdom deficit of 4.2 per cent of GDP – but their interpretation is genuinely disputed, and the accounting frameworks that generate them were not constructed to describe a sovereign state. Second, the objections to independence on transition grounds vary substantially in evidential strength and should not be aggregated: the trade-dependency objection is robust and largely independent of contested assumptions, whereas the decommissioning-liability objection is materially weaker once decommissioning tax relief and the multi-decade expenditure profile are taken into account. Third, the criticisms directed at the existing settlement are logically independent of the case against independence, and are not answered by it.

I conclude that the available economic evidence does not select between the constitutional outcomes under consideration. Both the unionist and the independence positions depend on counterfactuals that the published statistics cannot adjudicate, and the constitutional question turns additionally on considerations of democratic legitimacy, consent and risk tolerance to which economic analysis is not responsive. I recommend no constitutional outcome, and instead specify what each position would be required to demonstrate in order to be assessed on the evidence.

title: Hours of Labor as a Universal Burden Metric: Applications Across Planning, Policy, and Demographic Analysis
