detail.abstract: Household economic burden is typically measured through fragmented indicatorsrent-to-income ratios, cost-of-living indices, tax tables, transportation expenses, or health care premiums-none of which capture the lived reality of how much labor a household must expend each month to meet essential needs. This paper applies a unified, human-scaled metric: hours of labor required for basic household sustenance. By converting all major expenses and time losses into labor hours, the framework reveals the true burden households face across regions, occupations, and demographic groups. Using this metric, the paper demonstrates practical applications across seven domains: real estate and relocation decisions, workforce mobility and salary comparisons, taxation, health care systems, transportation and commuting, subsistence labor in mixed economies, and debt service. In each domain, the hours-of-labor metric exposes structural differences that traditional monetary comparisons obscure, enabling burden-neutral relocation analysis, effective wage comparisons, cross-jurisdiction tax evaluation, international health care burden assessment, and integrated household cost modeling. The result is a comprehensive tool for planners, policymakers, employers, and researchers seeking to understand and reduce total household burden. By reframing economic conditions in terms of time rather than money, the metric provides a transparent, intuitive, directly comparable, and easily comprehensible measure of household wellbeing, suitable for analysis across regions, occupations, demographic groups, currencies, and time.

title: On the Transmission of Purchasing Power Parity in a Group Setting
affiliations: The Karl Brunner Institute, University of Leicester UK - Department of Economics and Bank of Greece

detail.title: On the Transmission of Purchasing Power Parity in a Group Setting

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Greece Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Two characteristics of recent empirical studies on purchasing power parity (PPP) are that they have (1) examined whether PPP holds for individual countries and (2) investigated separately the respective roles of price adjustment and nominal exchange rate adjustment in bringing about PPP, with the magnitude of price adjustment estimated under fixed exchange rate regimes, and the magnitude of nominal exchange rate adjustment estimated under floating rates. We develop an extension of the Johansen reduced rank regression procedure, which we apply in a panel context. This extension allows us to both test the PPP hypothesis and to estimate the adjustment coefficients in a full panel more efficiently than in previous studies which use single-country data. We also extend the PPP model to allow differences between floating and fixed exchange rate regimes to test whether the adjustment process is different in the two regimes.

detail.abstract: Frontier economies face macro-financial risks that are dynamic, nonlinear, and interconnected. Sri Lanka's post-restructuring stabilization has restored a degree of external-sector confidence, but continued exposure to commodity-price shocks, exchange-rate pressure, domestic debt-market constraints, and financial-system linkages creates a need for forward-looking policy-support tools. This paper develops an integrated operations research framework for macro-financial resilience in Sri Lanka. The framework has three modules. The first uses a Markov regime-switching model and stochastic optimization to guide official reserve allocation across macro-financial states. The second models the domestic financial system as a directed network and applies a clearing mechanism to identify contagion channels under localized liquidity or solvency shocks. The third formulates domestic liability issuance as a sparse optimization problem that balances funding needs, refinancing risk, market-impact costs, and yield-curve stability. Stylized simulations illustrate how regime-aware reserve allocation may reduce drawdowns under external shocks, how network-clearing models can reveal vulnerabilities hidden by aggregate banking indicators, and how sparse issuance can reduce maturity fragmentation in the domestic debt market. The paper contributes by adapting quantitative finance and operations research tools to macroprudential policy, reserve management, and sovereign liability planning in a frontier-economy setting.

detail.abstract: A bank trades off a fire-sale discount against a default risk. The liquidation path is arithmetico-geometric. The model derives this path from an endogenous microstructure. detail.abstract: Crop diversification is a sustainable and cost-effective strategy with various benefits for agricultural systems and the overall livelihood of the farmers. This study focuses on crop diversification in Bangladesh, a significant rice producer facing challenges from climate change and geographical variability. The research was carried out in Mithapukur Upazilla, Rangpur district. Face-to-face interviews were employed to collect primary data. A pre-tested structured questionnaire was used to interview 122 farmers. We attempted to examine the degree of crop diversification using Simpson Diversification Index and Ogive Index. The average Simpson Index and Ogive Index were found to be 0.729 and 3.925, respectively, indicating that most of the studied farmers are having a high degree of crop diversification. Further, we found a total of 34 types of crops were cultivated in the study area. To analyze the determinants of crop diversification a Tobit model was employed. The study revealed that age, education, household size, farm experience, non-farm income, credit, and mobile access to agricultural information are major predictors of crop diversification. The study further highlights various farmer motivations for crop diversification. Most of the farmers cited reducing financial risk as the primary reason. Following that, we looked into several problems that farmers face when diversifying their crops. Pests and diseases had the highest index score of 205, demonstrating their enormous impact on farming. Finally, farmers' suggestions to encourage crop diversity were reported. The highest-ranking recommendation, with 122 responds, is for high-quality fertilizers and pesticides, underlining their significance to farmers. This study is anticipated to simultaneously address four pressing challenges in Bangladesh, including the eradication of poverty, enhancing farmer livelihoods, establishing food self-sufficiency, and ensuring nutritional balance. The study's findings will thus be critical in supporting the Bangladeshi government in taking the required efforts to address agriculture's issues and improve farmers' status.

detail.abstract: Cooperatives are one of the pillars of Indonesia's national economy, founded on the principles of mutual cooperation and kinship, aiming to improve the welfare of members and society at large. However, despite the increasing number of cooperatives, many have not been able to develop sustainably due to problems such as poor management, lack of member participation, limited capital, and low digital literacy. This paper aims to examine the definition, objectives, functions, roles, and principles of cooperatives, as well as to analyze the factors influencing their growth and development in the modern era. The method used is a literature study by reviewing various relevant sources including laws, books, and scientific journals related to cooperative development in Indonesia. The findings show that cooperatives in Indonesia have experienced significant growth in terms of number of members, assets, and economic contributions, particularly in the trade, agriculture, financial services, and creative industry sectors. Modern cooperatives have also evolved beyond savings and loan institutions into complex socioeconomic empowerment vehicles that support MSMEs through access to capital, training, and market networks. Nevertheless, cooperatives continue to face considerable challenges, particularly in adapting to digitalization, strengthening governance systems, and regenerating active members. The implication of this study is that the sustainability of cooperatives in the digital age requires synergy between management, members, government, and society through improved human resource quality, transparent governance, and continuous digital innovation, while still upholding the core cooperative values of togetherness, mutual cooperation, and economic democracy.

detail.abstract: This paper models Treasury intermediation as a two-tier problem between primary dealers and non-dealer final holders, in which the two tiers face opposite-signed constraints. The presence of opposite-signed constraints-which I call constraint polarityallows for a characterization of the relative effectiveness of purchases and swap lines that differs from the standard framework. The introduction of inventory memory generates a delay in the movement of the binding margin. The framework accounts for the March 2020 policy sequence and the low take-up of repo funding. The model is illustrative; the threshold is an empirical object.

title: The Vanishing Stabiliser: A Regime Shift in the Term Premium's Role for Financial Conditions Transmission
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Vanishing Stabiliser: A Regime Shift in the Term Premium's Role for Financial Conditions Transmission

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: I quantify the disappearance of the Treasury term premium (TP) as an automatic stabiliser of United States financial conditions. Using a 60-month rolling estimation on monthly Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) data from January 1994 to January 2026 (N = 385), I identify the break date as July 2010 via the interior-sample supremum of the rolling |t|-statistic on βv t = β(VIX×TP), consistent with the Andrews (1993) Quandt likelihood ratio (QLR) criterion. Minimum detectable effect (MDE) analysis establishes that at 80% power the study can detect any stabilising effect exceeding 0.0174-37% of the pre-2010 coefficient-ruling out effects of economically meaningful magnitude. Non-inferiority tests applied to the hypothesis that the post-2010 stabiliser equals at least half its pre-2010 size yield t_NI = 5.11 (p < 0.001). The March 2022 rate-normalisation window-in which the Federal Reserve raised the policy rate by 525 basis points and the TP recovered to positive territory-provides a natural experiment: the rolling coefficient remained near zero through early 2026, ruling out a cyclical explanation. I argue that three structural changes-the Federal Reserve's transformation into a dominant duration absorber through large-scale asset purchases (LSAPs), the growth of risk-parity strategies that mechanically reverse the flight-to-duration dynamic, and the expansion of the price-insensitive Treasury investor base-jointly explain the break's persistence. Across six robustness specifications, the cross-regime t-statistic is-3.85 (p < 0.001). Financial conditions indices (FCIs) and stress-test models retaining a pre-2010 TP weight carry quantifiable model risk.

title: Stochastic Escape Dynamics and Systemic Fragility in Liquidity Networks: A Cusp-Catastrophe Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Stochastic Escape Dynamics and Systemic Fragility in Liquidity Networks: A Cusp-Catastrophe Framework
detail.abstract: A stochastic potential-theoretic framework for systemic financial risk is developed within the methods of nonlinear statistical physics. Network fragility is modelled as a scalar order parameter F governed by a quartic double-well potential V(F; η, θ) = F 4 /4-ηF 2 /2-θF, derived from cusp catastrophe theory under two observable control parameters, namely transmission efficiency η and structural friction θ. The equilibrium manifold F 3-ηF-θ = 0 admits bistability when the discriminant 4η 3-27θ 2 is positive. Applying Kramers escape-rate theory to the associated overdamped Langevin equation yields a closed-form mean first passage time to systemic collapse, valid in the weak-noise regime 2ΔV/σ 2 ≫ 1. Critical Slowing Down, the divergence of local relaxation time as the system approaches bifurcation, is established as a theorem: variance and autocorrelation time both diverge as V″(F₀) approaches zero, providing real-time early-warning signals computable from market data. A dynamic capital rule minimising the escape probability is derived from the Fokker-Planck formulation of the escape problem.

title: Do Opportunity Zones Decrease Municipal Bond Reliance? Evidence from School District Bonds

detail.title: Do Opportunity Zones Decrease Municipal Bond Reliance? Evidence from School District Bonds

detail.abstract: Opportunity Zones (OZs), introduced through the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of December 2017, aim to stimulate economic growth in distressed communities by offering tax incentives to private investors. While these incentives attract private capital, they may also influence municipal revenues, raising important questions about their impact on public financing-particularly in the context of school district bonds, which represent a significant share of municipal bond issuance. Despite the importance of this issue, prior research has not examined how placebased policies affect the municipal bond market. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing the effect of OZs on the cost and issuance of school district bonds. Using a difference-indifferences (DiD) methodology, I show that while OZs do not significantly affect bond offering yields (a measure of issuance cost), they lead to a 21.5% reduction in bond issuance. This suggests that private capital inflow through OZs reduces municipalities' reliance on external public financing. The study provides new insights into the interaction between public and private financing within the framework of economic development programs like Opportunity Zones.

detail.abstract: Passive investing moves the stability threshold, but the direction of the move depends on the direction of strategic response. Replacing Green's linear mean-reversion assumption with Haddad et al.'s estimated pass-through lowers the Lyapunov threshold from 0.87 to 0.731 and the Feller threshold from 0.91 to 0.856. Positive feedback, as in ETF arbitrage, raises them to 0.988 and 0.992. Across countries, higher passive shares imply earlier instability. ECB (2024) documents that a 1 percentage point increase in passive ownership raises euro area stock correlation by about 0.005.

detail.abstract: Shadow banking is a chain. The chain passes assets and funding from one layer to the next. This paper adds feedback. Feedback turns the chain into a second-order system. The stability condition is γν < 1/(4 cos 2 (π/(K + 1))), where K is the chain length. The infinite-chain limit K → ∞ gives γν < 1/4. In the 2008 window, the ABCP proxy fell. The intermediary capital ratio fell. Under an illustrative mapping, the product γν rose by a factor between 1.49 and 1.91, depending on the base period. title: The One-third Rule: Passive Investing and the Moving Threshold of Financial Stability

detail.abstract: Passive investing lowers the mean-reversion speed nonlinearly. Replacing Green's linear assumption with Haddad et al.'s estimated pass-through and endogenizing volatility, the Lyapunov threshold falls from 0.87 to 0.732 and the Feller threshold from 0.91 to 0.852. The HHL correction accounts for most of the shift; the volatility feedback provides an additional downward push. Across countries, higher passive shares imply earlier instability. ECB (2024) documents that a 1 percentage point increase in passive ownership raises euro area stock correlation by about 0.005. Our thresholds suggest these effects become systemic at lower passive shares than previously estimated.

title: Evaluating Employer Intentional Torts in Ohio: Practical Lessons from Camara v. Gill Dairy for Workers' Compensation Practitioners

detail.title: Evaluating Employer Intentional Torts in Ohio: Practical Lessons from Camara v. Gill Dairy for Workers' Compensation Practitioners

declarations.declarationOfInterest: John D. Hance IV is an attorney at Garvin & Hickey, LLC in Columbus, Ohio, focusing on employer defense in workers' compensation and intentional tort matters. The author co-authored the Brief of Amici Curiae Ohio Chamber of Commerce and Ohio Alliance for Civil Justice in Camara v. Gill Dairy, L.L.C. before the Supreme Court of Ohio. These materials were prepared for the Ohio State Bar Association (OSBA) Advanced Workers' Compensation Seminar for educational purposes and reflect solely the author's independent legal analysis, not the institutional positions of his firm, clients, or amici.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or external financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. Preparation of these course materials was conducted independently in connection with the author's presentation at the Ohio State Bar Association Advanced Workers' Compensation Seminar.

detail.abstract:
In Camara v. Gill Dairy, L.L.C., the Supreme Court of Ohio addressed the heightened liability framework governing workplace injuries under R.C. 2745.01. While the Court eliminated the Twelfth District’s extra-statutory requirement that a claimant prove an employer made a conscious decision never to reattach a removed safety guard, it resolved the dispute by finding sufficient circumstantial evidence of affirmative detachment during maintenance. In doing so, the Court sidestepped the long-standing intermediate appellate split between districts recognizing pure maintenance omissions under R.C. 2745.01(C) and those limiting statutory liability strictly to physical extraction or bypass.
This article examines the operational mechanics of R.C. 2745.01 in the aftermath of Camara. It analyzes how the Court's application of Evidence Rule 301 burden-shifting permits claimants to survive summary judgment through circumstantial maintenance inferences, effectively blurring the statutory line between active misfeasance and passive nonfeasance. The article contrasts civil intentional tort litigation against administrative Violation of Specific Safety Requirements (VSSR) proceedings under Article II, Section 35 of the Ohio Constitution, evaluating differences in culpability standards, adjudicative forums, statutes of limitations, and insurability. Through four common industrial equipment scenarios, it charts the substantive "guarding gap" confronting practitioners across administrative and civil dockets. Finally, it details the commercial insurance coverage risks established by Hoyle v. DTJ Enterprises, Inc. and evaluates the broader constitutional debate surrounding whether Ohio's common-law intentional-tort doctrine can remain reconciled with statutory workers' compensation exclusivity.

title: Liquidation Speed and Institutional Friction
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Liquidation Speed and Institutional Friction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: This paper studies how institutional friction affects financial stability across countries. A bank trades off a fire-sale discount against a default risk, and the liquidation path is written in arithmetic-geometric form. Institutional friction determines where the trade-off sits. As friction rises, total liquidation rises, and the system approaches a critical threshold. Beyond the threshold, the dynamics becomes nonlinear. The model is calibrated and simulated, and the mechanism is traced through three historical crises. A policy implication follows.

title: Structural Fragility and Escape Dynamics in Liquidity Networks

detail.title: Structural Fragility and Escape Dynamics in Liquidity Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: Standard asset-pricing theory treats liquidity as continuous and volatility as meanreverting. Empirical history reveals a different phenomenology: financial networks exhibit prolonged quiescence interrupted by sudden endogenous phase transitions. I develop a stochastic potential-theoretic framework for this phenomenology. Network fragility is modelled as a scalar order parameter F governed by a quartic double-well potential derived from cusp catastrophe theory under two observable control parameters: transmission efficiency η and structural friction θ. The equilibrium manifold admits bistability when the discriminant ∆ = 4η 3-27θ 2 is positive. Applying Kramers escape-rate theory to the overdamped Langevin dynamics yields a closed-form mean first passage time to systemic collapse in the weak-noise regime 2∆V /σ 2 ≫ 1. Critical Slowing Down is established as a corollary. Euler-Maruyama simulations with η = 2, θ = 0.1 confirm the Kramers prediction within 5%-9% for 2∆V /σ 2 ≳ 2.5, and quantify the breakdown of the weak-noise approximation as σ increases.

title: Not on Average, but at the Extreme: Differences in Disruptive Output under Block-Grant and Competitive Project Funding
affiliations: , Institutes of Science and Development, Chinese Academy of Sciences and Institutes of Science and Development, Chinese Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Not on Average, but at the Extreme: Differences in Disruptive Output under Block-Grant and Competitive Project Funding

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant approval no. L242341; application receipt no. 7247041644).

detail.abstract: Block-grant and competitive project funding are two different mechanisms for government science funding, and comparing their effects has long been a central question in the design of public science funding systems. Existing research mostly evaluates their effects at the mean, without clarifying the real differences between these two mechanisms. This paper combines a theoretical model with large-scale empirical analysis to examine these differences. We develop a model building on evidence that the informational value of prospective evaluation declines with a proposed research direction's distance from the existing knowledge and test its implications using roughly nine million chemistry publications from 2004 to 2022, linking funding records, disruption scores, textual novelty, and citation timing. Our analysis finds that (1) In terms of the mean disruption of the outcomes produced by the two mechanisms, the difference is not significant; (2) However, among the top 1% most disruptive publications in the same year, the block grant mechanism yields a 2.46-fold higher selection probability than its competitive counterpart; and (3) within this high-disruptive tail, papers funded through block grants also carry more novel language and receive slower post-publication recognition. The difference between the two funding mechanisms manifests in the right tail of the distribution where evaluability is weakest, rather than in the mean. Therefore, this distinction should be fully recognized in the selection of government funding mechanisms, and a reasonable funding portfolio should be adopted.

title: Overcoming Barriers to Inter-Municipal Collaboration Through Imaginary Future Generations: A Deliberative Practice on Carbon Neutrality and Disaster Risk Reduction
affiliations: The University of Osaka, The University of Osaka, Doshisha University and The University of Osaka - Graduate School of Engineering

detail.title: Overcoming Barriers to Inter-Municipal Collaboration Through Imaginary Future Generations: A Deliberative Practice on Carbon Neutrality and Disaster Risk Reduction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research (Research Project Numbers: JP20H00053，JP21H03671) from the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science.

detail.abstract: Collaboration between local governments is considered essential for addressing complex, long-term societal challenges such as climate change. However, such collaboration is not easy in practice, due to the difficulties of reconciling conflicting interests and building consensus. In this study, we adpoted "Imaginary Future Generations" (IFGs)-a framework that has been proved to reliably generate "futurability" in people and society-in deliberation practices involving employees of multiple municipalities, to verify the effectiveness of IFGs in promoting inter-organizational collaboration. We conducted deliberation practices with participants from the local governments of four Japanese cities. The participants discussed their vision of the future society in 2060 and measures for inter-municipal collaboration on policies relating to carbon neutrality and disaster prevention from the perspectives of both current generations and 2 IFGs. We analyzed the results of these discussions together with data from questionnaires administered to the participants. We found that the application of IFGs changed perceptions about the future of society and societal challenges, leading to the formulation of more long-term and concrete visions of the future. With IFGs, discussion participants showed a greater willingness to actively tackle collaboration barriers and challenges relating to assessment methods and administrative procedures. Additionally, their policy proposals tended to shift from mere incremental measures within existing systems to more comprehensive and transformative action, such as wide-area disaster prevention systems. These findings indicate that adopting the perspective of future generations can serve as a foundation for a new approach for promoting inter-municipal collaboration in the effort to address societal challenges.

title: A Comprehensive Review on Boosting General Insurance in Sri Lanka through an Integrated Phygital and Machine Learning Framework
affiliations: , Staffordshire University and Staffordshire University

detail.title: A Comprehensive Review on Boosting General Insurance in Sri Lanka through an Integrated Phygital and Machine Learning Framework
detail.abstract: The general insurance sector in Sri Lanka is navigating a paradigm shift, driven by digital disruption and evolving consumer demands for seamless, omnichannel experiences. The traditional, agent-centric model is increasingly misaligned with the expectations of a digitally-empowered populace, while a purely digital approach fails to capitalize on the trust inherent in human interactions for complex financial products. This comprehensive review paper posits the "phygital" marketing paradigm-the synergistic integration of physical and digital touchpoints-as the optimal strategic response. We systematically analyze the potential of this approach to enhance customer acquisition, retention, operational efficiency, and brand loyalty. The primary contribution of this work lies in proposing a sophisticated, data-driven framework that embeds Machine Learning (ML) as the core intelligence layer of the phygital ecosystem. We provide a detailed taxonomy of ML applications, including supervised learning for predictive customer analytics, Natural Language Processing (NLP) for intelligent virtual assistants, and computer vision for automated claims processing. The paper further delineates a rigorous methodology for model development, validation, and deployment, addressing critical aspects such as feature engineering and model interpretability. A thorough analysis of implementation challenges, encompassing data integrity, algorithmic bias, and organizational change, is presented. By synthesizing contemporary literature with an advanced, practical ML framework, this study provides a definitive roadmap for insurers in emerging markets like Sri Lanka to transition towards an intelligent, resilient, and customer-centric future.

title: Unobservable Heterogeneity in the Marginal Propensity to Consume: Evidence from Korean Household Panel Data

detail.title: Unobservable Heterogeneity in the Marginal Propensity to Consume: Evidence from Korean Household Panel Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No coflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: Bank of Korea

detail.abstract: We estimate the distribution of the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) out of public transfers across Korean households, using fourteen linked waves of the Survey of Household Finances and Living Conditions (2012-2025; 132,965 household-year first differences). A finite mixture model finds that about three-quarters of households have a transfer MPC near zero while roughly a quarter respond with an MPC of 0.16, so the aggregate response is produced by a minority. That minority cannot be identified in advance: income, wealth, liquidity, debt and demographics jointly explain six to ten percent of the variation in responses, indistinguishable from the eight percent reported for the United States. Consequently a doubly robust targeting rule evaluated out-of-sample delivers less stimulus than a universal transfer. Six standard estimators applied to the same data yield average MPCs from 0.032 to 0.107, and unit conversions remove much of the apparent disagreement among published Korean estimates.

title:
Economic Persistence and Delayed Recovery in Pakistan

A discrete time Markov analysis of four interacting structural syndromes
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title:
Economic Persistence and Delayed Recovery in Pakistan

A discrete time Markov analysis of four interacting structural syndromes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known personal, financial, or professional relationships with any individual or organization that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research reported in this manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research was conducted without external financial support.

detail.abstract: Pakistan's repeated stabilization episodes raise a question that conventional descriptions of fiscal, energy, and governance problems leave unresolved: why can policy correction coexist with prolonged economic fragility? This paper develops a mechanism-based explanation linking four conditional syndromes: monetary tightening amplified by sovereign financing needs, electricity capacity and network mismatch, soft budget constraints in state owned enterprises, and fragmented governance. Official Pakistani statistics and World Bank enterprise data document the institutional setting. A three-state discrete time Markov model distinguishes convergence to a stationary distribution from first passage to recovery; a separate institutional learning model distinguishes agreement from policy quality. Analytical propositions show that administrative delay reduces the spectral gap without necessarily changing stationary welfare, while changes in the balance between reform and reversal alter the long run distribution. Illustrative simulations reduce expected first passage from distress to recovery from 91.67 to 10.42 model periods under combined improvements in transition speed and incentives. Coordination alone halves the passage time but leaves the recovery share unchanged at 14.29 percent; combined reform raises that share to 66.67 percent. These are transparent scenario results, not estimated Pakistani transition probabilities. The evidence supports the relevance of interacting constraints but does not identify their causal magnitudes. The central implication is that durable recovery requires both timely implementation and changes in the incentives that reproduce fiscal and productive stress.

detail.title: Proxy SVAR Identification of Oil and Sovereign Risk Shocks in the Venezuelan Economy

detail.abstract: This paper identifies oil and sovereign risk shocks in the Venezuelan economy with ex ternal instruments and delivers the resulting oil elasticity of growth to the scenario engine of the ARAP Sovereign–Bank Toolkit in the form the evidence supports, which is a set rather than a point. A four-variable system in real oil revenue, GDP growth, the sovereign spread and a banking-stress index over 1998Q1–2019Q4, identified by OPEC production shortfalls and by external EMBI+ credit events, finds that a one-standard-deviation negative oil supply shock lowers GDP by 2.3 percentage points at four quarters and widens the spread by 310 basis points, 28–29% more than the recursively identified responses of the companion Bayesian VAR, and that an adverse sovereign risk shock lowers GDP by 0.8 pp and raises banking stress by 0.42 standard deviations, the doom-loop channel measured directly. The oil–growth block is then re-estimated on the toolkit’s corrected quarterly GDP series through 2026Q2, with the within-quarter innovation of Brent as the external instrument, and every instrumented elasticity is reported with the Montiel Olea Pflueger effective F, an Anderson–Rubin set and a wild-bootstrap interval in place of a homoskedastic first-stage gate. Within the VAR the instrument is strong (effective F of 623) and the proxy identification differs from the recursive one only on impact, where it removes an endogenous production component and lowers the impact response from 0.47 to 0.21 pp per 10% shock; the peak of 1.05 pp at one quarter and the cumulative effect of 3.3% of GDPcoincide with the linear local projection (peak 1.09 pp) and are bracketed by its state-dependent versions (1.22 pp in the crisis regime, 0.47 pp in the normal regime). The single-equation one-year elasticity that the scenario engine consumes, instrumented by predetermined Brent news, is weakly identified (effective F of 14.4 against a critical value of 23.1): the 2SLS estimate of 2.98 pp is three and a half times the OLS estimate of 0.86, the Anderson–Rubin set is [1.46, 6.20] and the wild-bootstrap interval [0.46, 16.7]. Sub-sample elasticities of 0.06, 0.24, 0.23 and 0.12 around a full-sample 0.35, and a proxy response that doubles across 2014, document the instability that makes the set, with the regime selecting its relevant end, the object carried downstream.

title: Measuring sentiment news with transformer-based language models
affiliations: University of Pisa, , Corte dei Conti - Italian Court of Audits, University of Pisa and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Measuring sentiment news with transformer-based language models
detail.abstract: Measuring sentiment from financial news is a central task in economics and finance, yet most existing indicators rely on dictionary-based approaches that infer sentiment from word counts and only partially capture context, negation, and semantic structure. This paper proposes a framework for constructing daily news mood indices using transformer-based language models and evaluates whether they better represent sentiment than dictionary-based alternatives. Using 143,755 financial news articles from Factiva, we classify sentiment at the sentence level with FinBERT and aggregate these predictions into article-level and daily sentiment measures through alternative normalization schemes. We compare the resulting indices with benchmark measures based on Shapiro et al., 2022 and Barbaglia et al., 2025. A central contribution is the validation of alternative sentiment measures against human judgments. We conducted an incentivized annotation exercise in which 444 participants evaluated a validation subsample of 588 financial news articles. Consensus ratings from independent human evaluations serve as an external benchmark for assessing the quality of automated sentiment measures. Across correlation, regression, and classification exercises, transformer-based measures show stronger agreement with human judgments than vocabulary-based alternatives and perform substantially better in distinguishing positive, neutral, and negative articles. Overall, the results suggest that incorporating contextual information through transformer-based language models produces sentiment measures that more closely reflect human assessments of financial news.

title: Finish the Job: Completing Canada’s Capital Markets Reform Agenda
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Finish the Job: Completing Canada’s Capital Markets Reform Agenda
detail.abstract:
• Parliament discontinued funding for the Canadian Securities Transition Office in 2021, bringing an end to Canada’s most ambitious effort to establish a national securities commission, create a national framework for managing capital markets systemic risk, and strengthen the regime for the criminal enforcement of securities laws. The decision left important elements of the country’s financial stability architecture unfinished.
  • Canada remains an outlier among major advanced economies in lacking a statutory authority responsible for the comprehensive management of systemic risk in capital markets. Following the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, peer jurisdictions established dedicated frameworks for managing systemic risk, while Canada’s reform effort was never completed.
  • Canada should revive key elements of the unfinished reform agenda. Establishing a national capability to identify and manage systemic risks in capital markets would improve financial stability. Stronger investigation and prosecution of serious securities offences would also enhance investor confidence and support economic resilience.

title: The Vanishing Hedge The Term Premium and Financial Conditions Transmission after 2010

detail.title: The Vanishing Hedge The Term Premium and Financial Conditions Transmission after 2010

detail.abstract: The Treasury term premium once hedged equity volatility: when VIX rose, investors fled to duration, compressing the term premium and cushioning financial conditions. This paper documents that the hedge disappeared. Using a 60-month rolling estimation on monthly FRED data (1994-2026, N = 385), I identify July 2010 as the break date through the interior-sample supremum of the rolling |t|-statistic on β(VIX × TP). Minimum detectable effect analysis rules out any residual hedge exceeding 0.0174 (37% of the pre-2010 coefficient) at 80% power. Non-inferiority tests reject any residual hedge at least half the pre-2010 size (t = 5.11, p < 0.001). The hedge does not return during the 2022-2023 rate-normalisation window. A pre-2010calibrated financial conditions index mis-signals the direction of the term premium's contribution during a combined VIX-duration shock.

detail.abstract:
Wealth distribution tables show which generation holds the most assets, but they do not measure which
generation is economically influential. This paper introduces the Generational Economic Transfer Model
(GETM), a composite index that measures generational economic influence from four components:
existing wealth, intergenerational transfers, productivity/technology, and demographic participation. In
the general formulation, a generation's influence at time t is GEI_g,t = (W_g,t + T_g,t) × P_g,t × D_g,t,
where transfers are linked to the wealth of older generations through an intergenerational transfer ratio
λ. The framework is applied illustratively to U.S. data — Federal Reserve Distributional Financial
Accounts for wealth, BLS 2024 labor‐force participation rates, and Cerulli/Merrill projections of wealth
transfers through 2048 — for three generational groups: Baby Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials
plus Generation Z. The headline result is a ranking reversal across specifications: Baby Boomers lead the
wealth‐only ranking, Generation X leads the current‐influence ranking, and Millennials plus Generation Z
lead the projected ranking that includes future transfers. A 3×3 sensitivity analysis over transfer and
technology scenarios shows that the ranking is conditional rather than structural. GETM is presented as a
measurable and testable framework, not a final predictive model; its assumptions and the need for
time‐consistent estimation are stated explicitly.

title: Regulatory Governance of Telehealth Scaling Across State Borders: A Health Equity Analysis of Rural Communities in the United States

detail.title: Regulatory Governance of Telehealth Scaling Across State Borders: A Health Equity Analysis of Rural Communities in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external or institutional funding.

detail.abstract: Telehealth expanded rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic and is now part of routine care in the United States, but the rules deciding who may deliver that care still depend on where a patient is physically located, because medical licensure is set state by state. This essay examines how state-based licensure requirements shape telehealth access, continuity of care, and health equity for rural, medically underserved communities, and reviews the policy tools available to reduce cross-border regulatory friction. Drawing on peer-reviewed research, federal agency reports, and primary regulatory sources from 2017 through 2026, it finds that rural communities face compounding barriers, including clinician shortages, hospital and obstetric unit closures, and gaps in broadband access, that limit telehealth's reach exactly where it could help the most. Interstate licensure compacts and temporary Medicare waivers have expanded cross-state telehealth access unevenly, and much of that access still depends on short-term congressional extensions rather than a stable federal framework. A durable, equity-oriented approach, combining wider licensure compacts, stable federal Medicare telehealth policy, and continued broadband investment, is needed to protect continuity of care in rural, medically underserved communities.

title: Mandatory ESG Disclosure and Stock Price Crash Risk: Global Evidence from Staggered Regulatory Adoption
affiliations: Monash University - Monash University Malaysia, North South University, Monash University Malaysia,  and

detail.title: Mandatory ESG Disclosure and Stock Price Crash Risk: Global Evidence from Staggered Regulatory Adoption
detail.abstract: We examine the effect of the staggered implementation of mandatory environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure regulations on future stock price crash risk worldwide using a difference-in-differences framework. We find that mandatory ESG disclosure significantly reduces future crash risk, with results robust to alternative difference-in-differences designs, placebo tests, model specifications, crash-risk measures, and the exclusion of U.S. firms. Channel analyses provide evidence consistent with several behavioral pathways. Mandatory ESG disclosure reduces subsequent tax avoidance and overinvestment, both of which are associated with higher future crash risk, and improves ESG performance, particularly environmental and governance performance, which is associated with lower tax avoidance. These findings are consistent with mandatory disclosure strengthening external scrutiny, constraining opaque and inefficient managerial behavior, and limiting the accumulation of adverse firm-specific information. The reduction in crash risk varies with the institutional environment and regulatory design, with stronger effects outside the IFRS reporting regime, under weaker government effectiveness but stronger public enforcement, following prior voluntary disclosure, and under more comprehensive and immediate implementation. Overall, our findings provide global evidence that mandatory ESG disclosure reduces the risk of future stock price crashes through multiple behavioral channels and that its effectiveness depends on the institutional and regulatory environment.

title: Fixing Equal Pay Law: From Endless Litigation to Fair Pay by Design

detail.title: Fixing Equal Pay Law: From Endless Litigation to Fair Pay by Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A

detail.abstract:
Protracted, opaque and costly, the system fails its users. This report considers two key questions in relation to the UK's equal pay regime: first, what is wrong with it, and second, what can be done to fix it? While the first question often elicits extensive responses about procedural delays, complex law and lack of bite, it is the second which has proved more challenging. Are there changes that could be made to the law and procedure which would significantly improve the delivery of justice? Alternatively, or additionally, should the UK learn from other jurisdictions and reconsider the fundamental premises of its approach?

These are the questions this report aims to tackle. We do this by looking at three elements: (i) the substantive cause of action, (ii) procedure and remedies, and (iii) positive obligations.

We begin by considering the substantive cause of action where there remain ambiguities, needless complexity and unfair narrowness. The ambiguity lies in not only what actually constitutes equal value but also the material factor defence and what is permitted. Complexity can be found in the burden of proof which zig-zags back and forth between claimant and respondent. The narrowness concerns the scope of comparison. Contracted out workers cannot be compared against those In-house. Further, the all-or-nothing approach means that two roles are either equal or they are not. This leaves gaps in protection for those women whose work is, of say 75% the value of the man’s but is paid only 50%. And, of course, the equal pay regime is confined to discrimination based on sex, not on other protected characteristics – or none.

Discrete reform to the cause of action could help reduce complexity and uphold legal certainty. These reforms might include codifying acceptable material factors, requiring employers to take steps to uphold equal pay when outsourcing and introducing limited hypothetical comparators when it comes to proportionate pay inequalities. However, ultimately, reform in this sector is unlikely to transform the experience of equal pay claimants.

We then turn to look at procedure and remedies. The individual approach to bringing claims, and the adversarial litigation model, continue to pose a significant obstacle to claimants. Informational asymmetries prevent workers knowing that they have a claim altogether. Where they are aware of a potential claim, they can expect delays or impasses owing to satellite litigation around time limits, interminable job descriptions and (challenges to) the reports of independent experts.

To speed up the resolution of equal pay issues, we therefore propose incentivisation for out-of-court settlement, page limits for job descriptions, addressing the material factor defence sooner and giving the tribunal more discretion over limitation periods. Those we interviewed complained of the unpredictable outcomes of independent expert reports and so we propose a uniform methodology for equal value assessments. Then, at the final hearing, tribunals must be more willing to order an equal pay audit where breaches are found. Such procedural and remedial reform has the potential to reduce delays and increase transparency. However, alone, they are unlikely to be transformational.

This brings us to our final and most ambitious proposal: strengthening positive obligations on employers. We recommend that larger employers should be required to carry out equal pay audits which proactively consider the value of all roles within the organisation to form the basis of a fair pay scale. This process should not be static. Inspired by the Icelandic model, we propose a periodic 'certification' process whereby audits must be approved every three years.

Certification would then serve an important signalling function to workers and customers about the nature of the employer/service provider. It would also come with incentives such as priority in public procurement. While a positive obligation regime is designed to prevent unfair pay disparities arising in the first place, a reformed regime of individual litigation (addressed in the first two sections) would remain a necessary fallback. Rather than making all-or-nothing determinations that two roles are of equal or unequal value, 'fair pay' considers whether there is, across all roles within an organisation, a fair relationship between value and pay.

This report was published by UNISON on 17 September 2026.

title: How Do Cancer Care Experts Weigh The Importance Of Health Inequities In Cancer Incidence And Mortality: An Exploratory Multi-Criteria Expert Consensus Across Six Cancer Sites

detail.abstract:
Background: Cancer control has traditionally emphasized biological and behavioral risk factors,while socioeconomic and structural determinants have received less attention in population-levelprioritization. In Chile, it remains unclear how cancer-related experts prioritize these determinantsrelative to established risk factors, and whether their relative importance diﬀers between cancerincidence and mortality.

Methods: We developed an integrated Fuzzy Delphi–OWA–TOPSIS framework to prioritizepopulation-level cancer determinants across six cancer sites in Chile. Forty variables were selectedfrom the literature and evaluated by a panel of oncology experts using a four-level linguistic scale.Expert judgments were aggregated using an Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) operator andrepresented through Best Non-fuzzy Performance (BNP) scores. TOPSIS was then applied usingc onsensus intensity, consensus quality, and cross-cutting knowledge coverage as criteria. Rankingstability was assessed through sensitivity analyses varying the OWA aggregation parameter andTOPSIS criterion weights.

Results: The prioritization produced distinct patterns for cancer incidence and mortality. Forincidence, the highest-ranked variables included active smoking, advanced age, education, mul-tidimensional poverty, and alcohol consumption. For mortality, multidimensional poverty, loweducational level, Years Lost due to Disability, unemployment, and smoking occupied the highest positions. Across OWA parameter values, Spearman correlations ranged from 0.773 to 0.964 forincidence and from 0.920 to 0.992 for mortality. Across alternative TOPSIS weighting schemes,correlations ranged from 0.781 to 0.964 for incidence and from 0.910 to 0.976 for mortality.

Conclusions: Expert prioritization diﬀered between cancer incidence and mortality, with socioe-conomic and structural determinants receiving greater prominence in the mortality ranking. Theresults indicate that population-level assessment of cancer determinants should distinguish betweenfactors associated with cancer incidence and those prioritized in relation to mortality. The proposed framework provides a structured approach for integrating expert judgment, linguistic uncertainty,and multi-criteria prioritization in the analysis of population-level cancer determinants.

title: Entropic tilting of forecasts to SPF histograms: analytics & applications
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland and

detail.title: Entropic tilting of forecasts to SPF histograms: analytics & applications
detail.abstract: We develop a direct approach to incorporating survey density forecasts into model-based predictive distributions. Histogram forecasts from the U.S. Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) carry rich nonparametric information about expected outcomes, but existing methods rely on moment-based approximations that discard part of it. We instead tilt entropically to the histogram probabilities themselves, matching them exactly. After reformulating the single-histogram problem, we derive a new analytic characterization of the multiple-histogram case, solved by Iterative Proportional Fitting and applicable to simulated densities from essentially any model. Applying the method to real-time forecasts from a Bayesian VAR with time-varying volatility, we find that tilting to SPF histograms substantially improves accuracy relative to the model’s baseline forecasts, especially during the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. The gains extend beyond the variables the SPF targets, improving forecasts for other variables in the system as well.

detail.abstract:
The general rule is that inventors should only obtain one patent per invention. But this rule is not explicitly spelled out in the statute. Courts have long imposed a gloss on the Patent Act to limit inventors from patenting the same thing twice. The justifications have varied over time, but a prominent one relevant to pharmaceutical patenting is that a second—double—patent would likely extend the term of protection for the invention.

This chapter explores the implications of double patenting in the pharmaceutical industry. It examines why the phenomenon exists, whether it continues to be an issue now that patent terms are tied to filing date, reviews the empirical literature on drug entry associated with double patenting, and considers whether double patenting in itself is the problem. In doing so, the chapter explores Congress’s role in facilitating—even encouraging—double patenting through permissive continuation and nonobviousness rules. Finally, the chapter uses this background to consider the costs and benefits of proposed responses to double patenting.

detail.title: Reimagining Companion Animal Rights: A Theory of Contractualized Property Ownership

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts to declare

detail.abstract:
Companion animals present a conundrum. Across legal systems, animals are classified as personal property and thus subject to human ownership. Yet they offer invaluable love, affection, and friendship—things that ordinary chattels simply cannot provide. Despite their social and emotional significance, the sale of companion animals is governed by the same legal principles that govern furniture, automobiles, or household appliances. Once title passes, the seller’s interest ends. Whether the animal receives adequate care, is abandoned or neglected, or suffers abuse is largely left to the owner’s private discretion.

The dominant response has therefore been to enact stronger welfare protections and tighten public enforcement. In the United States, all fifty states prohibit some form of animal cruelty, and some impose affirmative duties concerning food, shelter, social interaction, and veterinary care. But those laws are systematically underenforced. Mistreatment often occurs within private homes, while public authorities lack the information, resources, or incentives to prosecute violations. In other jurisdictions, including China, legislatures have not prioritized animal welfare and may never enact meaningful protections. Those twin institutional failures—which we term “enforcement gaps” and “legislation gaps”—leave animal suffering undetected, unremedied, and effectively beyond the law’s reach.

This Article turns to private ordering as a potential solution. Animal rights theorists have long characterized property status as the source of animals’ subordination. We challenge the premise that property provides only a vehicle of dominion and control. Where public authorities are unwilling or unable to act, property can become a source of protection. Because property consists of a divisible, customizable “bundle of sticks,” parties can contract for ongoing welfare obligations, monitoring rights, transfer restrictions, and preventative remedies even after title transfers. That contractual division of ownership reflects a longstanding principle of property law: title can pass without transferring every stick in the bundle.

Building on that insight, this Article proposes a standardized but modular regime of contractual governance for companion animal welfare. Private contracting can narrow enforcement gaps by generating information and civil remedies before harm becomes irreversible, while addressing legislation gaps by supplying standards that public law has failed to provide. More broadly, this Article articulates a theory of contractualized owner-ship: the use of contract to reconfigure property entitlements into a con-tinuing regime of governance after transfer.

title: Do Markets Discipline the Adoption of Dangerous Technology?
affiliations: University of Oregon - Department of Finance and University of Oregon

detail.title: Do Markets Discipline the Adoption of Dangerous Technology?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest

detail.abstract: We study adoption when technological disaster risk rises with both capability and deployment. Under a common survivable disaster, adopters suffer the same proportional loss as non-adopters. But disasters select high-capability states, precisely where adopters do best, and marginal utility is high in those states, so markets pay for adopters' payoffs. Adoption is therefore a hedge, though no firm avoids the disaster, and the hedging motive raises adoption, which raises disaster probability in turn. Equilibrium deployment exceeds not only its social optimum but the level that would obtain with no disaster risk at all. The hedge depends on the loss being common: damage confined to adopters taxes them directly, and extinction removes the payoffs that make the hedge worth holding, so both restrain adoption instead. Empirically, we find that option-implied tail risk now moves with stock prices in a manner broadly consistent with a potential common AI disaster.

title: Does Fertility Stabilize At Low Levels? Evidence from Period, Cohort, and Subnational Data
affiliations: Research Institute for Compassionate Economics (r.i.c.e.), University of Texas at Austin, University of Texas at Austin and Hunter College (CUNY)

detail.title: Does Fertility Stabilize At Low Levels? Evidence from Period, Cohort, and Subnational Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: As global total fertility approaches replacement, a key focus of population science has been to characterize the contemporary "post-transition" stage in low-fertility societies. Many population projections used by international and government agencies assume that, in today's low-fertility societies, future fertility rates will stop declining and roughly stabilize. This paper assesses evidence for an equilibrium point or rebound from low levels. Using phase diagrams to plot the average rate of change in fertility as a function of its level, we find that there is no robust evidence for a stable equilibrium point or for a systematic fertility rebound, at any level conventionally assumed. This is true across a range of data sources and fertility measures: United Nations data on period total fertility rates for all country-years from 1950 to 2023; Human Fertility Database data on completed fertility for cohorts born between 1935 and 1975 in 31 countries; and fertility rates in subnational geographies in Japan, India, and the United States. We reconcile these results with a prior literature that documented fertility reversals among some low-fertility countries in the early 2000s. Our findings provide an empirical basis for reexamining the equilibrium and rebound assumptions embedded in widely-used population projections.

title: Do AI Trading Agents Herd? Experimental Evidence and Financial Stability Implications
affiliations: and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No declaration of interest

detail.abstract: This paper provides micro-foundations for understanding how AI-powered trading affects market dynamics. We conduct laboratory-style experiments using large language models to replicate classic studies on herd behavior in trading decisions. Our results show that AI agents rely less on market trends and more on private information compared with human traders. However, exploring variations in the experimental settings reveals that AI agents can be induced to herd optimally when explicitly guided to make profit-maximizing decisions. In other experimental variations, we show that AI agents are not purely algorithmic, but have inherited some elements of human conditioning and bias.

detail.abstract: This essay argues that the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, the first binding international treaty on artificial intelligence (AI), is best understood as expressive hard law. The Convention opened for signature in September 2024 and drew broad signatory support, yet as of September 2026, no country has ratified it, it remains short of entry into force, and its Conference of the Parties has not begun its supervisory work. Treaty form gives States a public way to affirm shared commitments to human rights, democracy, and the rule of law in AI governance, while broad obligations and a flexible implementation model preserve wide domestic room for regulatory choice. Because AI carries exceptional public salience, and because the Convention is the first binding instrument in a field long governed by soft law, signing it confers a visible benefit on States at little regulatory cost, a benefit States visibly spend, citing the fact of signature as evidence of alignment with rightsprotective AI governance even as ratification remains distant. Signature is therefore doing more expressive work than regulatory work. The essay develops this claim through the Convention's design, the politics of delayed entry into force, and article 18 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, which gives signature legal significance before full operation through the interim duty to respect the treaty's object and purpose. The space between signature and the Conference of the Parties' supervision reveals a separation among three elements in international AI governance, namely, legal form, acceptance of shared principles, and submission to international supervision.

title: From Climate Finance to Climate Resilience: A Critical Review of Climate Change, Cryosphere Hazards, Disaster Risk Reduction and Financing Lessons from the 2026 Bhotekoshi Flash Flood in Nepal
affiliations: School of Environmental Science and Management and School of Environmental Science and Management

detail.title: From Climate Finance to Climate Resilience: A Critical Review of Climate Change, Cryosphere Hazards, Disaster Risk Reduction and Financing Lessons from the 2026 Bhotekoshi Flash Flood in Nepal
detail.abstract:
The catastrophic flash flood and debris-flow event that struck Bhotekoshi and downstream areas on 26 August 2026 provides an opportunity to examine these interconnected risks. Importantly it raises questions about whether existing climate-finance and disaster-risk-financing systems are sufficiently prepared to reduce such risks.This paper presents a review of the relationship between climate change cryosphere hazards, disaster risk reduction, climate finance and long-term resilience in Nepal. The study uses the 2026 Bhotekoshi disaster as a contemporary case lens to explore how climate change drives cryosphere hazards that increase disaster risk reduction challenges. The authors also discuss how climate finance can build long-term resilience in Nepal. The review focuses on five themes: (1) climate and cryosphere change; (2) GLOF, flash-flood and cascading mountain hazards; (3) climate adaptation and disaster-risk reduction; (3) climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction; (4) climate and disaster risk financing; and (5) post disaster recovery, loss and damage and Build Better.
The review points out that Nepal has taken steps in creating climate and disaster-risk groups and in getting international adaptation money. However, the research also shows that there are still differences between what happens during disasters and the money that is available to deal with them. There is no use of financial tools that come before a disaster happens. Also, there are problems with how different organizations work. It is hard to get climate money down to the level. The Bhotekoshi disaster shows how hard it is to handle disasters that happen one, after another. These kinds of disasters can involve glaciers, rocks, dirt and rivers all at the time.
The paper says that Nepal problem is not about getting more money for climate issues but about making sure the money leads to real reductions in risks. An idea called the Climate Finance–DRR Resilience Nexus is suggested. This idea connects things like watching for dangers giving warnings getting communities ready building strong buildings having money set aside before a disaster responding quickly when something happens rebuilding after making things better, than before and planning for the future. The study ends by saying Nepal needs to stop reacting after disasters happen and instead start planning ahead. This means looking at risks having money ready stopping problems before they get bad getting ready acting early rebuilding in a strong way and thinking about the long term.

detail.abstract: We study how artificial intelligence affects welfare in general equilibrium when production requires both finding and solving problems. Unsolved problems are unexploited opportunities or unmet needs that agents find in a congested sector. Problems are solved in layered hierarchies in which agents can ask for help. Firms may adopt a replicable AI agent in either activity. AI deployed in solving problems splits the human knowledge hierarchy: greater AI capability affects the layers above AI, whereas lower cost affects the layers below it. Either form of progress can lower welfare by reallocating solvers to the congested finding sector. A tax on finding corrects this distortion; when this is not possible, the optimal tax on AI can be positive or negative, depending on its effect on the congestion externality.

title: How Bureaucratic Capacity Shapes Regulatory Outcomes: Evidence from Land Use in Los Angeles
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles - Anderson School of Management, University of Connecticut and California State University

detail.title: How Bureaucratic Capacity Shapes Regulatory Outcomes: Evidence from Land Use in Los Angeles

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed in this paper are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the Ziman Institute. All errors are our own.
declarations.funderStatement: We thank the UCLA Ziman Institute for Real Estate and Urban Economics for financial support of this research.

detail.abstract: While land use regulation is central to urban development outcomes, local review and approval of development proposals remains a black box. In this paper, we use the documentary record of the Los Angeles City Planning Commission from 2018 to 2026 to assess local regulatory practice. We apply large language models to convert 29,000 pages of agendas, minutes, and public correspondence into a structured dataset of 818 development decisions. Findings show that outright denial of development is rare (1.2% of all cases), and that the more salient margin is delay. We then investigate factors that predict delay. Other things equal, project physical characteristics have little explanatory power in our models. Instead, public opposition and process-based frictions such as how unusual a project is matter more. Results indicate that a doubling of the number of opposition letters increases the log odds of delay by 0.154, and a one standard deviation higher atypicality increases the log odds of delay by 0.404. Further results indicate that utilization of pre-defined state and local housing incentive programs mitigates the effects of public opposition and atypicality, suggesting a streamlining effect of templatized programs. The results provide rare field evidence that bureaucratic capacity, not statutory rules alone, shapes the pace of urban development.

title: Measuring Bank Funding Costs: A Korean Across-the-Curve Credit Spread Index
affiliations: , Seoul National University and Yonsei University - School of Business

detail.title: Measuring Bank Funding Costs: A Korean Across-the-Curve Credit Spread Index

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: We construct an across-the-curve credit spread index (AXI) for the Korean credit market. AXI measures the average unsecured funding cost of major commercial banks across maturities and thereby captures aggregate credit risk in the Korean debt and money markets, providing information that risk-free benchmarks inherently omit. The index is constructed as the average of long-term and short-term components: the long-term AXI aggregates credit spreads on senior unsecured bank bonds using issuance and transaction-volume weights, while the short-term AXI applies the same weighting scheme to certificates of deposit issued by major commercial banks. Our results show that the Korean AXI effectively captures major credit stress episodes. Furthermore, its co-movements with CDS spreads, exchange rates, and international yield differentials demonstrate that AXI reflects both domestic credit conditions and global financial pressures. Overall, the index offers a comprehensive, credit-sensitive adjustment to the Korean Treasury curve.

title: Electrocoagulation-Assisted Hydrocycloning Treatment of Deep-Sea Mining Sediment Plumes: A Novel Front-End Particle-Conditioning Strategy
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Coastal and Offshore Engineering, State Key Laboratory of Coastal and Offshore Engineering, State Key Laboratory of Coastal and Offshore Engineering, State Key Laboratory of Coastal and Offshore Engineering, Ocean University of China, Ocean University of China and State Key Laboratory of Coastal and Offshore Engineering

detail.title: Electrocoagulation-Assisted Hydrocycloning Treatment of Deep-Sea Mining Sediment Plumes: A Novel Front-End Particle-Conditioning Strategy
detail.abstract: Near-bed sediment plumes generated by deep-sea mining contain abundant fine particles that can remain suspended for extended periods and are difficult to classify effectively using hydrocyclones alone. This study investigates electrocoagulation (EC) as a novel front-end particle-conditioning technology to assist hydrocycloning treatment. Multiphysics modeling, fixed-volume screening, continuous-flow experiments, multi-mineral evaluation, and coupled electrocoagulation-hydrocycloning (EC-HC) tests were performed under controlled cold and saline conditions. The model revealed a clear spatiotemporal relationship between the transport of Al-based hydrolysis products and the growth of equivalent particle size. Under the representative Al/graphite condition, EC achieved approximately 82-89% turbidity removal across three multi-mineral simulated plumes, while SEM observations showed morphologies consistent with fine-particle attachment, lamellar bridging, and composite aggregation. Compared with direct hydrocycloning, EC pretreatment redistributed and narrowed the particle-size distribution of the hydrocyclone underflow, increasing the 5-20 μm fraction from 42.38% to 50.57% rather than causing uniform particle coarsening. The EC stage required approximately 0.041 kWh m-3 of direct-current energy. These findings support EC as a compact auxiliary process upstream of hydrocyclone classification and provide a technical basis for vehicle-mounted, near-source EC-HC systems that integrate plume capture, particle conditioning, classification, and concentrated-solids return, thereby supporting lower-disturbance deep-sea mining operations.

title: Algorithmic Lending and Financial Fragility
affiliations: Stephen M. Ross School of Business, University of Michigan and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Algorithmic Lending and Financial Fragility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A

detail.abstract: We develop a model of algorithmic lending in which a FinTech lender uses a neural network and alternative data to screen borrowers. The FinTech competes with a less-informed bank, and borrowers differ in creditworthiness. Low-quality borrowers can manipulate the characteristics observed by the algorithm, which contaminates the algorithm's training data. The resulting feedback loop between the algorithm's learning and borrowers' manipulation incentives can generate multiple equilibria or prevent an equilibrium from existing. With multiple equilibria, identical borrower populations can face different lending standards and default rates, leading to self-confirming algorithmic discrimination. When equilibrium does not exist, lending standards and manipulation can fluctuate over time despite unchanged fundamentals. To improve stability in the credit market, regulators can implement circuit breakers, restrict FinTechs' data choice, and mandate that lending models are benchmarked against less sophisticated alternatives. Regulation focused on the algorithm itself is unlikely to be effective.
