detail.abstract: A thermodynamic framework for socioeconomic systems introduces "social temperature" as a metric for collective sentiment and volatility. Building on bionomics and econophysics, it treats the economy as a thermodynamic system, where entropy measures disorder (e.g., inequality) and temperature captures social energy. By incorporating ESG criteria, sentiment analysis, and information entropy, this approach seeks to improve economic forecasting, optimize policy efficiency, and explain phenomena like financial bubbles or productivity-stress relationships. Bridging natural and social sciences, it offers a shared language to unify fragmented fields while addressing ethical concerns such as data privacy and manipulation. The goal is to foster collaboration in testing and refining a model that transforms socioeconomic analysis into a cohesive, adaptive discipline.

title: "Interpretation" : How price formation works when the same public evidence supports more than one reading

detail.title: "Interpretation" : How price formation works when the same public evidence supports more than one reading

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) brought valuable discipline to performance claims while leaving implicit the activity that connects public evidence to valuation: interpretation. This paper makes interpretation (an investor's mapping from public evidence to expected payoff) explicit and models prices as the capital-weighted balance of the resulting forecasts. It finds that efficiency tests examining specified uses of the evidence can return clean results while an interpretation outside those uses earns systematic alpha, which limits what the tests can establish about the market as a whole. The model also links expected interpretive alpha to the improvement in price accuracy from giving an interpretation a little more influence. Where evidence has determinate implications, shared interpretation restores the familiar question of whether those implications are fully reflected in price, helping explain the relevance of eventstudy findings in such settings. Extension from clean test results to a market-wide efficiency verdict, however, requires interpretive completeness as a third hypothesis, alongside efficiency and the return benchmark, ruling out profitable improvements even from methods not yet invented. For imperfect prices, it requires justification for a limit to profitable interpretation and for concluding that current prices have reached it. Together these arguments support retiring the binary efficiency verdict as an omnibus research objective and studying instead how interpretations develop, influence prices and improve through competition, the subject of a companion paper ("Competition").

title: Scale and Local Information in Housing Markets: A Graph-Laplacian AVM Benchmarked Against Machine Learning
affiliations: Neoval

detail.title: Scale and Local Information in Housing Markets: A Graph-Laplacian AVM Benchmarked Against Machine Learning
detail.abstract:
Automated valuation models are often presented as a trade-off between predictive accuracy and explicit econometric structure. We test this claim in repeated prospective evaluations of 13,100 house sales in Inner West Sydney across 35 quarterly cutoffs from 2015 to 2023. We compare a graph-Laplacian hedonic model with LightGBM gradient boosting, random forest, and conventional hedonic regressions. The graph model achieves the lowest median absolute percentage error: 9.75%, compared with 10.02% for the best LightGBM benchmark, which is supplied with features based on previous and nearby sales. Although modest, the 0.27-percentage-point difference is statistically resolved (95% bootstrap confidence interval: 0.07–0.51).

More broadly, the comparisons show that accuracy depends less on whether a model is econometric or machine-learning than on how it captures fine local variation in persistent dwelling premia. Restricting the training region improves plain LightGBM, but most of that benefit disappears once local sales histories are supplied. A penalized coordinate surface substantially improves a conventional hedonic regression; once hedonic coefficients and time indexes vary regionally, the geographic extent of the fit matters little. Local model structure, engineered sales histories, and local fitting are therefore partly substitutable routes to spatial detail. The graph model additionally estimates local price indexes, persistent dwelling effects, and their uncertainty as explicit model quantities. It therefore retains transparent structural outputs without sacrificing point-prediction accuracy, although at substantially greater computational cost than engineered boosting.

title: Reading a Published Record: Alphabet-Indexed Readability, the Value of Labels, and the Collapse of a Search History into One Observation

detail.title: Reading a Published Record: Alphabet-Indexed Readability, the Value of Labels, and the Collapse of a Search History into One Observation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
A reader of a published record faces three radii at a fixed confidence level: the structural radius from the record fibre, the readability radius of the record law on a stated encoding alphabet, and the radius a reading attains. The readability radius is the infimum over all readings measurable on that alphabet, and never exceeds half its own fibre diameter. Coarsening can only raise it, so the gap between a reader and the ideal record splits into coding and reading terms. Without labels the minimax radius equals the zero-information constant exactly. Under extremal reporting, inside the exact Gumbel location submodel, one record carries Fisher information one about log quality. A reader is judged against the ceiling of its own alphabet.

ChatGPT and Codex (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic) were used to assist with Lean formalization and supporting proof work, polish the text, and organize the literature. The core research ideas were developed by the author. The scope and limitations of the machine-checked results are specified in this paper. The author takes full responsibility for the final manuscript.

title: "Competition" : A theory of markets in which alpha is a feature rather than a bug

detail.title: "Competition" : A theory of markets in which alpha is a feature rather than a bug

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) saw alpha as a defect: a profitable reading of shared public evidence not yet eliminated by competition. This paper proposes the Competitive Market Hypothesis (CMH), in which alpha rewards price correction, and models how an interpretive opportunity is produced, deployed and eroded. An investor who finds a superior interpretation earns expected alpha while giving her reading more weight would improve price accuracy. When her whole position trades at one clearing price, a larger position moves the price against her on the whole holding, so she limits her position and leaves part of the correction to others. Other investors adopting the same reading narrow the remaining gap, giving her a reason to share the superior interpretation she has found. CMH proposes that this process repeats: competition gives existing interpretive opportunities a finite half-life while new interpretations create fresh ones. Prices tend to improve through this process without converging on any idealised terminal state. Alpha in this model is therefore seen as an essential productive feature of competitive markets, rather than a bug.

title: The Problem Generation Framework of Switch Measure Theory: Five Illustrative Results, 137 Open Problems, Five Deep Problems, and the Impossibility Boundary

detail.title: The Problem Generation Framework of Switch Measure Theory: Five Illustrative Results, 137 Open Problems, Five Deep Problems, and the Impossibility Boundary

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
This paper establishes the problem generation framework of Switch Measure Theory, and presents five illustrative results and five deep problems of the framework. The framework takes the problem generation operator G as its core tool and the order operators G^k and the graded meta-ization operator Ψ_k as its recursive structure, and systematically generates open problems on the proved theorem basis T = {T_1, …, T_29} (numbering consistent with Tang 2026aw) and the extension direction set D = {D_1, …, D_7}. On the precise meaning of “generation”: the “generation” in this paper refers to structured classification, not algorithmic generation—G is a criticizable classification framework (see Section 2.2 for details).
Five illustrative results: (1) the computational complexity upper bound of the switching degree is O(p²) (or O(p^ω) if the precision-matrix form is used), with the exact lower bound left as an open problem; (2) a strict bijection between no-horizontal-step switching sequences and Dyck paths, with the sequence count equal to the Catalan number C_n; (3) via the one-sided inverse Lipschitz condition, the two-step estimator satisfies a minimax lower bound consistent with the boundary information lower bound c=1/8; (4) the switching spectrum satisfies a third-moment Lyapunov condition in high dimensions, and is asymptotically normal; (5) the concrete quadratic form ĥ(τ) produces a pseudo-peak under heterogeneous configurations.
Three naming proposals: switching manifold, switching category, regime algebra—these are the author’s convenient names for certain mathematical objects, not claims of terminological priority.
Five deep problems (in three levels): (Level One, firmly grounded) D1 non-regular Le Cam theory, D2 the optimal rate spectrum of nonparametric continuous switching; (Level Two, requiring precise construction) D3 the classifying space of the switching category, D4 a sheaf-theoretic interpretation of no false peaks; (Level Three, exploratory) D5 homotopy characterization of the three-valued η. These five problems do not occupy Q numbering or Ω numbering.
Order structure: first-order problem set P_0 (100 concrete problems), second-order problem set P_1 (Ω_1–Ω_8), third-order problem set P_2 (Ω_9–Ω_29), three cross-border problem sets with distinct object types (P_cat, P_Gödel, P_term), and the system-level problem set P_sys (Ω_30–Ω_34).
This paper proposes a total of 137 open problems: 100 first-order problems, 29 meta-problems, 3 cross-border problems, and 5 system-level problems. Of these, 54 are marked as N-level (first-of-their-kind problems). In addition, this paper proposes five deep problems and eight impossibility conjectures (IMP-01–IMP-08). Together with Tang (2026av, system outline) and Tang (2026aw, mathematical outline), this paper constitutes the complete program of Structural Regime Mathematics.
Research Paradigm Statement: The core methodology, research direction, and final decisions were independently directed by the author. DeepSeek assisted with code implementation, data presentation, and text drafting. The author takes full academic responsibility for the final content.

detail.abstract: This book is the inaugural volume of "Architects of Economic Thought," a series of critical intellectual monographs on leading economists whose research programs have shaped modern economic theory and policy. Volume I reconstructs and critically assesses the research program of Ricardo J. Caballero (Ford International Professor of Economics, MIT), organized around three pillars: (I) lumpy microeconomic adjustment and its aggregate consequences for investment, employment, and prices; (II) safe assets, global imbalances, and financial crises; and (III) monetary policy as risk management through financial markets. The book closes with a critical synthesis examining open tensions within this research program and its largely unexplored implications for economies that are structural net demanders — rather than suppliers — of safe assets, including Chile, Latin America, and Central/Eastern Europe. Every factual and bibliographic claim has been verified against original published sources.

title: Innovation: Market Failures and Public Policies
affiliations: University of Toronto - Strategic Management and Stanford University

detail.title: Innovation: Market Failures and Public Policies
detail.abstract: This is an invited chapter for the forthcoming Volume 4 of the Handbook of Industrial Organization.  We summarize the state of the literature on the economics of innovation and highlight open policy questions.  We first articulate the key market failures in markets for innovation, and then discuss how both scientific norms and market-oriented policies help overcome those market failures.  We close by discussing recent work on the diffusion of inventions as well as on the links between innovation and inequality.

title: Labor-Force Heterogeneity and Asset Prices: the Importance of Skilled Labor
affiliations: , University of Minnesota, University of Texas at Dallas and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Labor-Force Heterogeneity and Asset Prices: the Importance of Skilled Labor
detail.abstract: We introduce labor-force heterogeneity in a neoclassical investment model. In the baseline model, we highlight the fact that labor adjustment costs are higher for high skilled workers than for low skilled workers. The model predicts that the negative hiring-expected return relation should be steeper in industries that rely more on high skilled workers because firm's hiring responds less elastically to changes in the discount rate when labor adjustment costs are higher. In an extended version of the model we show that the previous prediction also holds in the presence of additional sources of  labor-force heterogeneity such as higher wage rigidity of high skilled workers. Empirically, we document that the negative hiring-expected return relation is between 1.7 and 3.2 times larger in industries that rely more on high skilled workers, than in industries that rely more on low skilled workers. This result is robust: it holds in U.S data, in international data, across sub-samples, and in both firm-level and portfolio-level analyses. Taken together, our results show that labor-force heterogeneity affects asset prices in financial markets.

title: The Effect of Non-Wage Competition on Corporate Profits
affiliations: , Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Finance, Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics and University of Toronto

detail.title: The Effect of Non-Wage Competition on Corporate Profits
detail.abstract:
Most S&P 500 corporations disclose that their profits depend on non-wage competition for worker talent via workplace amenities like work-life balance. We quantify this dependence using a labor market matching model with endogenous amenities. When productive (unproductive) firms provide the amenities demanded by workers at a lower cost, firm quality becomes more (less) dispersed relative to worker quality, which results in higher (lower) firm profits due to competition. This cost advantage is identified with data on wages, worker satisfaction, and firm scale. Calibrating our model to Glassdoor surveys, a 1% increase in workers’ non-pecuniary preferences raises firm profits by 0.6%.
